confirmedFindings.title: Control-channel and fd-pass writes have no SIGPIPE protection: a vanished peer kills the process instead of surfacing as a caught write failure
confirmedFindings.evidence: Control::_send documents 'Closes the channel (and returns false) on a write failure (a vanished peer)' and wraps syswrite in eval, but eval cannot catch SIGPIPE: writing to a socket whose peer closed delivers SIGPIPE and the default action terminates the process before EPIPE is ever returned. Test2::Collector::Util::Socket::write_frame does `local $SIG{PIPE} = 'IGNORE'` for exactly this reason; Control::_send and FdPass::send_fds (IO::FDPass::send -> sendmsg) do not. App::Yath2::Command::spawn installs `$SIG{$sig} = sub { $ctl->send_signal($sig) }` (spawn.pm line 334) and sets no PIPE handler.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: The spawn supervisor crashes (or the runner kills its stage). The user presses Ctrl-C in the still-attached `yath spawn` command; the INT handler calls $ctl->send_signal('INT'), syswrite hits the closed socket, SIGPIPE kills the yath command silently — no 'supervisor closed the control channel' message, no exit-status handling, wrong exit code, and pre_exit_hook/terminal restoration never run. Same for send_fds when the target dies between connect and recv (sendmsg on 2nd/3rd fd raises SIGPIPE, killing the command mid-handoff).
confirmedFindings.proposal: Add `local $SIG{PIPE} = 'IGNORE'` around the write loop in Control::_send and around the IO::FDPass::send loop in send_fds, matching write_frame, so peer death surfaces as EPIPE -> close/croak as documented.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: The Ctrl-C-after-supervisor-crash scenario is real but its window is narrow: the command blocks in read_message/sysread and normally sees EOF from the dead peer within milliseconds, after which the CLOSED guard (Control.pm:203) makes send_signal a safe no-op; the signal handler must fire between peer death and EOF processing. The more reliably triggerable instances are (1) send_fds at spawn.pm:280 when the supervisor dies between target_connect and completing recv_fds of all 3 descriptors (e.g. its eval at JobLauncher.pm:126-136 fails and it _exit(1)s mid-receive; the command's 2nd/3rd sendmsg then raises SIGPIPE and kills the yath command mid-handoff), and (2) the supervisor side: SIGPIPE at send_hello (JobLauncher.pm:161) after the fork at line 143 kills the supervisor and permanently orphans the spawned process group, since the on-command-death kill logic (lines 174-181) never runs. Proposed fix (local $SIG{PIPE}='IGNORE' in Control::_send and around the IO::FDPass::send loop, matching Debug.pm:365) is correct and also covers the supervisor side.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Two corrections to the finding's scope: (1) the interactive STDIN fd-pass path is NOT exposed — App/Yath2/Options/Debug.pm:365 sets `local $SIG{PIPE} = 'IGNORE'` in the accept loop, and its dynamic scope covers the send_fds call in _interactive_pass_stdin (Debug.pm:389), so "a test that dies mid-handshake" is already handled there; only spawn.pm's send_fds call is unprotected. (2) A secondary consequence worth noting: SIGPIPE killing the detached JobLauncher supervisor before its control-loop close-detection runs can orphan the setsid'd spawned child, violating the "spawned process is bound to its command" contract (ARCHITECTURE.md §4.8) — though the window (client death between connect-back and hello) is tiny. Fix is exactly the proposal and is cheap: `local $SIG{PIPE} = 'IGNORE'` around the syswrite loop in Control::_send and the IO::FDPass::send loop in send_fds, matching the existing pattern in t2clib/Test2/Collector/Util/Socket.pm:66. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this (grep for SIGPIPE finds nothing relevant), so it needs its own small task or can ride along with any spawn/interactive follow-up chunk.

confirmedFindings.title: Final line without trailing newline is silently dropped by all Stream/JSONL readers (done flag never set)
confirmedFindings.evidence: File.pm read_line line 101: `return unless $self->{+DONE} || substr($line, -1, 1) eq "\n";` holds back an unterminated final line until `done` is set, but nothing in any read path ever calls set_done — it exists only as a public setter (only t/unit/.../Stream.t calls it). Stream::read()/poll(), stream_json_l_file(), and every downstream consumer (App::Yath2::Finder rerun file at Finder.pm:311-314, Command/failed.pm:57-62, Command/times.pm, Command/speedtag.pm, RenderLoop::JSONLFileProducer) read static complete files without setting done. Verified by execution: printf '{"a":1}\n{"b":2}' > y.jsonl; stream_json_l_file('y.jsonl', ...) delivered 1 record instead of 2; same result for the .gz variant.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A user supplies a rerun list (`yath test --rerun=file.jsonl`) or a log file (`yath failed log.jsonl`) whose last line is a complete JSON record but has no trailing newline (hand-written file, editor without final newline, truncated copy). The last record — often the harness_final rollup or the last failed job — is silently ignored: `yath failed` omits that failure, `--rerun` silently skips that test. No warning or error is emitted.
confirmedFindings.proposal: For bounded (non-tailing) reads, release the final unterminated line: e.g. stream_json_l_file and Stream::read should set_done(1) before the last poll (or read_line should treat a complete-at-EOF static read as done). Alternatively warn when a poll ends on a held-back partial line so the drop is visible.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Severity should be P3 rather than P2: JSONL files written by the harness itself are always newline-terminated (JSONL encode appends "\n"), and a byte-truncated log's final line is normally invalid JSON that would be skipped anyway (Finder uses skip_bad_decode => 1). The silent-loss case therefore requires an externally-produced or hand-edited file whose last line is complete JSON but lacks a trailing newline — real and silent, but narrow. The mechanism, cited lines, consumers, and proposal are all accurate as written.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix: in Util::File::read_line, treat EOF on a non-tailing read as done — or simpler, have stream_json_l_file and the bounded consumers (Finder rerun, failed, times, speedtag) call $stream->set_done(1) before polling, since they all read static complete files; alternatively emit a one-line warning when a poll ends holding a partial line so the drop is visible even in tailing mode. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this; the only tangential item is that JSONLFileProducer is slated for deletion when DB-based replay lands (TODO_TASKS.md ~line 974), which removes one consumer but not the Finder/failed/times/speedtag paths. Worth fixing in passing during the planned DB/logger overhaul since the reader is being touched anyway.

confirmedFindings.title: Legacy HARNESS- directive with missing arguments corrupts the result tree and dies 'Not a HASH reference', surfacing as a bogus test failure
confirmedFindings.evidence: _record has no guard for a directive with no arguments: bare '# HARNESS-META' gives $rest undef -> line 163 splits undef (uninit warning) -> $key undef -> lc(undef) at line 224 -> _append("meta.", undef): split /\./ on 'meta.' drops the trailing empty part, so the leaf 'meta' becomes an ARRAY [undef] instead of a subtree. A subsequent valid '# HARNESS-META foo bar' then does _append('meta.foo', ...) which executes `$node->{$p} //= {}` (no-op, meta is a true arrayref) and dereferences the arrayref as a hash -> dies 'Not a HASH reference at Legacy.pm line 305'. Verified by execution. Same pattern for bare '# HARNESS-TIMEOUT' (sets leaf 'timeout' => ['']) followed by '# HARNESS-TIMEOUT-EVENT 5', and bare '# HARNESS-NO' followed by '# HARNESS-NO-FORK'. TestFile.pm catches the die (eval at TestFile.pm:271) and stores it as _DIRECTIVE_ERROR, so the test file is reported as a synthetic FAILURE whose message is the internal 'Not a HASH reference at .../Legacy.pm line 305'.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A test file header contains a malformed legacy directive with no arguments (e.g. '# HARNESS-META' left over from an edit) plus any later directive under the same dotted prefix. The test is marked failed with the misleading internal error 'Not a HASH reference at .../Directives/Legacy.pm line 305' (plus uninitialized-value warnings on stderr) instead of a clear 'directive requires arguments' diagnostic — or, with the bare directive alone, a silently corrupted result tree (meta => [undef]) is handed to _apply_directives.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In _record, validate before dispatch: for 'meta' require both key and value (warn '_at' and return otherwise); for 'no'/'yes'/'use'/'timeout' require a non-empty feature/type and skip with a warning when absent. Never build a dotted path with an empty segment; optionally make _set/_append croak with a clear message on empty path parts.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two small corrections: (1) only the bare-META-then-valid-META case dies at Legacy.pm line 305 (_append); the TIMEOUT and NO variants die at line 282 (_set). (2) The user-visible message is even worse than claimed: TestFile.pm's _clean_err (line ~362) strips the trailing ' at <file> line N.' location, so the queued directive_error is just 'Not a HASH reference' with no location at all. Proposed fix (validate args in _record before building dotted paths; croak/warn on empty path segments in _set/_append) is appropriate.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fixes in passing: (1) the existing TODO_TASKS.md cleanup ticket converting Legacy.pm _record (lines 157-267) to a dispatch table is the natural place to add per-directive arg validation; (2) a one-line croak/warn on empty path segments in _set/_append (Legacy.pm:275-284, 298-307) with _at($file,$ln) context converts the die into a clear diagnostic; (3) #58's precedence rule (any HARNESS2: line makes legacy HARNESS- lines ignored) already shrinks exposure. confirmedFindings.title: Legacy parser warnings report wrong line numbers (counts only directive lines fed to it)
confirmedFindings.evidence: parse_line increments $self->{line_no} once per call and _at() embeds it in user-facing warnings ('Unknown harness directive ... at FILE line N.'). The only production driver, App::Yath2::TestFile::_scan_headers (TestFile.pm:307), feeds the Legacy parser ONLY lines matching /HARNESS-/ — unlike the new-grammar parser which is fed every line (TestFile.pm:280) and so has correct numbers. Therefore line_no is the count of legacy directive lines seen, not the file line number, yet the warning is formatted as a file position ('at t/foo.t line N.').
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A test file has its 3rd HARNESS- directive on file line 40 with a typo, e.g. '# HARNESS-RETRY twicw'. The user sees "Unknown 'HARNESS-RETRY' argument 'twicw' at t/foo.t line 3." and looks at line 3 of the file, which is unrelated — the diagnostic actively points at the wrong place.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Let the producer pass the real line number (parse_line($line, line => $ln)) or have TestFile feed every scanned line to the Legacy parser as it already does for the HARNESS2 parser (non-matching lines are cheap no-ops), so line_no matches file lines.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: The proposal's `parse_line($line, line => $ln)` would need a signature change (current signature is `parse_line($self, $line)`, Legacy.pm:112). The lower-friction fix is the finding's alternative: have TestFile feed every scanned header line to the legacy parser exactly as it already does for the HARNESS2 parser at TestFile.pm:280 — Legacy's parse_line returns early on non-matching lines (Legacy.pm:124), so this is a cheap no-op, and lines are already chomped so the embedded-newline croak (Legacy.pm:115) cannot fire.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheapest fix: in lib/App/Yath2/TestFile.pm (~line 307), feed every scanned header line to the Legacy parser exactly as is already done for the new-grammar parser (non-matching lines are no-ops), making line_no track real file lines; alternatively extend parse_line to accept an explicit line number. confirmedFindings.title: maybe_open_file/maybe_read_file TOCTOU: file deleted between -f check and open crashes (confess) instead of returning undef
confirmedFindings.evidence: maybe_open_file does `return undef unless -f $file; return open_file($file, $mode);` and open_file confesses on open failure ('Could not open file ...'). The 'maybe' contract (POD and all callers) is 'undef is returned if the file cannot be opened', and Util::File::fh() at File.pm:77 relies on `maybe_open_file(...) or return undef` for graceful handling of files that appear/disappear. In this multi-process harness, event/state files under the workdir are created by collectors and removed by cleanup while renderers/readers poll them via File objects, so the check-then-open window is crossed by a concurrent unlink.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A renderer/reader process polls a jsonl file via Test2::Harness2::Util::File::fh() at the same moment the owning process (or workdir cleanup on run teardown / CTRL-C) unlinks it: -f succeeds, the file is unlinked, open() fails ENOENT, and instead of fh() returning undef (poll returns 'no lines'), the reader dies with 'Could not open file ... No such file or directory', killing the polling loop mid-render.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Implement maybe_open_file by attempting the open directly and returning undef on ENOENT (e.g. `open(my $fh, $mode, $file) or return undef if $!{ENOENT}`), keeping the confess for other errors; drop the -f pre-check.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Scope note: fh() caches the handle per PID (File.pm:68), so the race only hits on the first successful open of a file (or after reset()) — exactly the poll-until-file-appears pattern, but it narrows exposure; most realistic triggers are run teardown/CTRL-C where the crashing reader was about to stop anyway, confirming P3. Fix refinement: map only ENOENT (and arguably ESTALE) to undef and keep confess for other errno values; also note open_file's compression branch (Util.pm:325) dies via IO::Uncompress::*->new with a module error variable rather than $!, so an ENOENT-tolerant rewrite must handle .gz/.bz2 paths too (simplest: keep the -f check AND additionally return undef when open fails with ENOENT).
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix as proposed: in maybe_open_file, attempt the open directly and return undef when $!{ENOENT} (keep confess for other errno), dropping the -f pre-check; route maybe_read_file through the same logic (its read_file->open_file path has the identical race at Util.pm:277-278). A handful of lines in lib/Test2/Harness2/Util.pm, no caller changes needed since the documented contract is already "undef if the file cannot be opened". No existing TODO_TASKS.md item covers this; it could ride along with any Util.pm touch. Note the compression branch of open_file (Util.pm:325, IO::Uncompress ->new) dies rather than confesses and would also need the ENOENT-undef treatment if .gz/.bz2 files can be maybe-opened.

acc_verdict.reason: Verified: maybe_open_file (Util.pm:334-338) and maybe_read_file (Util.pm:275-279) both do a `-f` pre-check then call open_file, which confesses on open failure (Util.pm:330). POD at Util.pm:707/717 documents the contract as 'undef is returned if the file cannot be opened', so an ENOENT confess inside the check-then-open window violates the documented contract. Util/File.pm:77 fh() relies on `maybe_open_file(...) or return undef` with no surrounding eval, and pollers (Util::File::Stream/JSONL via Queue.pm, Tester.pm, status.pm, run.pm) call fh() repeatedly until a file appears. Concurrent unlink is real and cross-process: Command/stop.pm:77 and kill.pm:48 remove_tree the workdir from a separate process, and Command/runner.pm:94 removes it on exit, while other processes may still be polling files in it; nothing (lock, single-writer, eval) protects the window. The failure path executes as described: -f true, unlink, open fails ENOENT, confess kills the polling loop.

sev_verdict.reason: The TOCTOU is real (Util.pm:336-337 does -f then open_file, which confesses at Util.pm:330), but the practical exposure is much narrower than the finding's scenario implies. (1) Util::File::fh() caches the handle per PID (File.pm:68), so the race window exists only at the very first successful open of each file per process; once opened, a concurrent unlink is harmless (POSIX keeps the fh readable). (2) The only live poll-a-file consumer of File::JSONL via fh() in normal operation is App::Yath2::RenderLoop::JSONLFileProducer, and it is used solely by `yath replay` on a static, user-supplied log file — the 2.0d event pipeline uses unix-socket services, not file polling, so there is no common path where a renderer polls a file another process deletes. No such file or directory") in a process that is already shutting down — a noisy death rather than wrong results, hangs, or data loss. That requires a microsecond-scale coincidence (unlink landing between -f and open on the first-ever open of that file in that PID) plus a reader active during teardown. Reachable in principle in supported configs (persistent runner + `yath stop`/`kill`), so not refuted, but it is a latent shutdown-window edge case: P3.

confirmedFindings.title: Value.pm init() does not call SUPER::init, bypassing the required-name check and the fh constructor argument
confirmedFindings.evidence: File.pm::init croaks "'name' is a required attribute" and moves the ctor 'fh' arg into _INIT_FH. Value.pm overrides init with only `$self->{+DONE} = 1;` and never calls $self->SUPER::init(), so Value->new() with no name is accepted silently, and Value->new(fh => $h) leaves the handle in $self->{fh} where fh() (which only consults _INIT_FH) never finds it.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Code constructs Test2::Harness2::Util::File::Value->new() with a missing/undef name (e.g. an unset settings path): construction succeeds instead of croaking; a later ->read confesses from open_file with an uninitialized-value warning and the unhelpful message "Could not open file '' (<)", far from the construction site. A caller passing fh => $handle gets reads from the named file (or undef) instead of the supplied handle, silently.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Have Value::init call $self->SUPER::init() before setting DONE.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Fix as proposed but preserve the deliberate DONE=1 override (Value files do not grow, so read_line must return unterminated final lines): sub init { my $self = shift; $self->SUPER::init(); $self->{+DONE} = 1; }. Note this quirk is inherited verbatim from the human-authored yath 1.x/legacy_pre_ai_2.0 code and the class has no production callers on 2.0d yet, so this is a hardening fix for future callers, not an active defect.

confirmedFindings.title: ByRun::get_coverage_tests swaps the changes_exclude_loads / changes_exclude_opens guards
confirmedFindings.evidence: Per the base-class contract (CoverageAggregator.pm POD and ByTest's touch docs), sub-key '*' means 'code outside a subroutine was executed' (i.e. the file was LOADED) and '<>' means 'file was opened via open()'. Options/Finder.pm defines changes_exclude_loads = "Exclude coverage tests which only load changed files" and changes_exclude_opens = "...which only open() changed files". ByTest.pm gates correctly (line 131 `unless ($changes_exclude_loads)` guards the '*' bucket pushed to froms{loads}; line 137 `unless ($changes_exclude_opens)` guards '<>' -> froms{opens}). ByRun.pm has the guards inverted: line 118 `unless ($changes_exclude_opens)` guards the '*' bucket (pushed to {loads}) and line 126 `unless ($changes_exclude_loads)` guards the '<>' bucket (pushed to {opens}). The bucket-to-name mapping ('*'->loads, '<>'->opens) is consistent everywhere; only ByRun's unless-conditions are swapped. (Same swap exists in reference/pre_ai_2.0, so it is a long-standing inherited bug, but it directly contradicts the option documentation and the sibling class.)
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath test --changes ... --changes-exclude-loads --cover-from coverage.json` (run-level/ByRun coverage source, dispatched via App::Yath2::Plugin::Cover::coverage_handler -> ByRun::get_coverage_tests). Tests that only load a changed module (only '*' hits) are still selected and run, while tests that open() the changed file (only '<>' hits) are silently dropped from the run even though the user never asked to exclude opens. --changes-exclude-opens has the mirror-image wrong effect. With ByTest (.jsonl) coverage data the same flags behave correctly, so the two coverage formats give contradictory test selections for identical data.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In ByRun::get_coverage_tests swap the two guards: gate the '*'/loads block with `unless ($changes_exclude_loads)` and the '<>'/opens block with `unless ($changes_exclude_opens)`, matching ByTest.pm and the option descriptions.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Finding is accurate as written, including line numbers and the note that the swap is inherited from reference/pre_ai_2.0. Proposed fix (swap the two unless-guards in ByRun::get_coverage_tests to match ByTest.pm) is correct. Only impact caveat: both flags default to 0, so the bug only manifests when a user explicitly passes --changes-exclude-loads or --changes-exclude-opens with run-level (ByRun/JSON) coverage data.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Fix is a trivial two-guard swap in ByRun::get_coverage_tests to match ByTest.pm. confirmedFindings.title: ByTest::finalize pushes wrongly-shaped records ({testname => rec} instead of rec) for tests still in progress
confirmedFindings.evidence: stop_test (ByTest.pm line 33) pushes the bare record `delete $self->{+IN_PROGRESS}->{$test}` (shape {test => $name, files => {...}, aggregator => $class}) onto COMPLETED. finalize (line 91) instead pushes `{$_ => delete $ip->{$_}}` — a wrapper hash keyed by test name, with no top-level 'test', 'files', or 'aggregator' keys. Every consumer expects the stop_test shape: (a) the file encoder writes it verbatim as a jsonl line; (b) Cover.pm coverage_handler (line 415) does `$agg = $set->{aggregator} // return;` so wrapped records are silently discarded when the coverage jsonl is read back; (c) Cover.pm annotate_event (harness_final branch, lines 225-249) does `$final = $aggregator->finalize()` then emits a run_coverage facet from `$final->[0]->{files}` / `->{testmeta}` guarded only by `if $final && @$final` — for ByTest leftovers both are undef, so a run_coverage annotation with files=undef, testmeta=undef is emitted into the event stream/log/DB. Identical code exists in reference/pre_ai_2.0, i.e. inherited, but no consumer anywhere handles the wrapped shape.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Run `yath test --cover-write=coverage.jsonl` and have any test never emit harness_job_end before harness_final (bail-out halts the run, test killed by timeout/SIGINT, truncated collection). At finalize the still-in-progress test's coverage is written as {"t/foo.t":{"test":"t/foo.t","files":{...}}}. A later `yath test --changes ... --cover-from coverage.jsonl` silently drops that record (aggregator key missing), so tests covering the changed files are NOT scheduled — changed code ships without its covering tests being re-run, with no warning. Additionally the same run emits a bogus run_coverage facet whose files/testmeta are undef.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In ByTest::finalize push the record itself: `push @{$cm} => delete $ip->{$_} for keys %$ip;` (the record already contains its test name). If flagging incompleteness is desired, set a key inside the record (e.g. $rec->{incomplete}=1) rather than changing its shape. Also consider guarding Cover.pm's run_coverage emission on `$final->[0]->{files}` being present.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: The trigger is narrower than claimed: timeout kills, bail-outs, and aborts DO get a real or synthesized harness_job_end (Driver.pm _render_abort, _render_completion:455 synth_job_end fallback, _finalize_live:555), so stop_test fires and the record is written correctly. The reachable leftover case is a collector that died without writing a terminal or final_state (skipped by Driver.pm:546's `next unless $c->{final_state} || status complete/finalized`), i.e. genuinely truncated collection. Since coverage artifacts from such broken runs are less likely to be fed back via --cover-from, practical impact is lower than the finding suggests: P3 rather than P2. Fix proposal is sound: push the bare record (it already carries test/files/aggregator), optionally with an incomplete=>1 marker, and guard Cover.pm's run_coverage emission on $final->[0]{files} being defined.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap one-line fix as proposed: `push @{$cm} => delete $ip->{$_} for keys %$ip;` — the record already carries `test`/`aggregator` keys (set in start_test, ByTest.pm:26), so the correct shape is self-describing; optionally set `$rec->{incomplete} = 1` inside the record. Also cheap: guard the run_coverage push in Cover.pm on `$final->[0]->{files}` being defined. Same bug exists in reference/pre_ai_2.0 (inherited from yath 1.x), so upstream/legacy users share the exposure.

confirmedFindings.title: QVF double-counts ECOUNT: buffered events are counted again on failed-job replay and job-end/harness events are counted twice
confirmedFindings.evidence: QVF::write increments $self->{+ECOUNT} (line 60) for every event it sees, including events it also forwards to SUPER::write, and Test2::Formatter::Test2::write increments ECOUNT again (parent line 265). Paths that hit both: (a) a failing job's whole buffer is replayed via `$self->SUPER::write(@{$_}) for @$buffer` (line 52) — each buffered event was already counted once when buffered, so a failing job with N events adds ~2N to ECOUNT; (b) every passing job's harness_job_end event goes through SUPER::write (line 56) AND line 60 (+2 per job); (c) every job_id-0/harness event (`!$job_id` branch) likewise counts twice. ECOUNT is user-visible: render_status (parent line 534) prints "Events: $self->{+ECOUNT}" in the status bar, and the `$show ||= 1 unless $self->{+ECOUNT} % 10` refresh cadence uses it. The update_active_disp __RENDER__ guard (line 27) protects the file/pass/fail stats from double counting but nothing protects ECOUNT. (Behavior is identical in reference/legacy QVF — long-standing.)
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath test --qvf` on a TTY with failing tests: the "Events: N" figure in the live status bar inflates by the full buffered event count of every failed job plus 2 per completed job, so N can approach twice the real number of processed events — a wrong count displayed to the user.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Skip QVF's own `$self->{+ECOUNT}++` for events that are (or will be) forwarded to SUPER::write, e.g. only increment when the event was merely buffered, or have the replay loop decrement/compensate; alternatively snapshot/restore ECOUNT around the replay and the SUPER::write calls.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One minor correction to claim (c): !$job_id events carrying harness_system facets are counted only once, because the parent write short-circuits at Test2.pm:258-261 (set_system_load + return) before its ECOUNT++ at line 265; all other !$job_id events are double-counted as claimed. Also note the failed-job replay includes the harness_job_end event itself (pushed at QVF.pm:41 before the branch), so the failing-job inflation is exactly the buffered count N, i.e. total 2N with no separate +2 for the end event. Impact is confined to non-verbose QVF mode (REAL_VERBOSE guard at QVF.pm:35 bypasses everything when -v is set) and is cosmetic: inflated "Events:" figure and a somewhat faster 1-in-10 status refresh.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix: in QVF::write, move `$self->{+ECOUNT}++` before the SUPER::write branches and have it fire only for events that were buffered-not-forwarded, e.g. snapshot ECOUNT before the replay/`SUPER::write` calls and restore it after (`local` won't work since ECOUNT must persist; save/restore explicitly), or simply delete QVF's own increment for the harness_job_end/!$job_id branches since SUPER::write already counts those. No TODO_TASKS.md ticket touches QVF, but any planned renderer/status-bar rework (the dbthoughts renderer overhaul) could absorb this one-liner. Behavior is identical in the legacy/reference QVF, so this is long-standing and has never generated a user report.

ECOUNT is user-visible via render_status "Events: N" (Test2.pm:534) and drives the %10 refresh cadence (QVF.pm:65). The __RENDER__ guard in update_active_disp (QVF.pm:27) protects only file/pass/fail stats, not ECOUNT. No guard, comment, or test indicates the inflation is intended.

confirmedFindings.title: _finalize_live waits the full 5s TAIL_TERMINAL_TIMEOUT per collector for jobs already settled by _render_aborted (serial, per job)
confirmedFindings.evidence: _render_aborted records the verdict keyed by job_id but never sets `$self->{+BY_UUID}{$uuid}{ended}` (it has no uuid). _finalize_live's sweep (Driver.pm:529-541) gates only on `next if $entry->{ended}` and then runs `until ($entry->{ended}) { ... last if (time-$start) > TAIL_TERMINAL_TIMEOUT; sleep 0.02 }` BEFORE the status/final_state check at line 545. An aborted job's collector never writes an events-file terminal (per Monitor.pm:525 'its collector will never report completion'), so ended can never become true and each such uuid burns the full 5 seconds, serially, even though its verdict was already settled by the aborted render. After the timeout the `next unless final_state || complete || finalized` check skips it anyway, so the wait accomplished nothing.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Live-tail mode (`--live`) run with -j8 where 8 tests stall and the watchdog aborts them (or run-timeout teardown aborts them). At end-of-run, _finalize_live stalls 8 x 5s = 40 seconds after the last output before printing the rollup/summary.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Skip the bounded wait for collectors whose job already has a settled verdict/aborted render (check $self->{+ABORTED_RENDERED}{$job_id} or $job->{verdict}), and/or move the `final_state || complete || finalized` status check before the wait loop as the non-live finalize sweep does.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Correct the failure scenario: hung tests do NOT reach _render_aborted (collector event_timeout finalizes them normally with a real terminal), and resource_timeout aborts fire only with no tests running. The pointless serial 5s-per-collector wait in _finalize_live occurs only for watchdog-aborted jobs whose collector emitted its 'starting' transition but died without finalizing — the SIGKILL grace fallback for a non-complying collector during yath abort/owner-drop/wind-down teardown, or a crashed collector — under --live (or interactive, which auto-enables live). Impact is a bounded end-of-run delay (5s per such collector, serial) with correct verdicts/exit code. Fix stands as proposed and is 1-3 lines: in the _finalize_live sweep, `next if $self->{+ABORTED_RENDERED}{$job_id};` (or `next if $job && $job->{verdict};`) before the until-loop, and/or hoist the line-546 status gate above the wait, mirroring the non-live sweep at Driver.pm:244-249. Severity lowered to P3: the prior P2 rationale assumed any hung test under --live triggers it, which the collector event_timeout path disproves; the surviving trigger (hard-killed/crashed collectors during an abort teardown, in live mode) is an unusual conjunction with latency-only impact.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix (1-3 lines): in the _finalize_live sweep, skip uuids whose job is already settled — e.g. `next if $job && $job->{verdict};` or `next if $self->{+ABORTED_RENDERED}{$job_id};` before the wait loop — or hoist the line-546 `final_state || complete || finalized` gate above the until-loop, mirroring the non-live finalize sweep (Driver.pm:244-249) which checks status first. Alternatively have _render_aborted mark ended on the collector's BY_UUID entry when the job_id↔uuid mapping is known. No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry covers this; worth fixing in passing with any Driver.pm renderer work.

sev_verdict.reason: Confirmed reachable: --live is a supported option (default off, but auto-enabled in interactive mode per App/Yath2/Options/Debug.pm:326-328), and watchdog/run-timeout aborts happen in normal use with hung tests. _render_aborted (Driver.pm:348) never sets BY_UUID{$uuid}{ended}, and _finalize_live (Driver.pm:529-541) runs the 5s bounded wait before the final_state/complete/finalized check at line 546, so each aborted job whose collector started burns a full serial 5s for nothing. confirmedFindings.title: Job-filtered replay sleeps 20ms per 1000-event batch because filtered-out batches are counted as idle
confirmedFindings.evidence: RenderLoop::iterate sets `IDLE = @events ? 0 : 1` from the producer's returned (post-filter) events (line 221) and start() sleeps IDLE_DELAY (0.02s) whenever IDLE (line 206). JSONLFileProducer::poll reads up to 1000 raw events but returns only those matching the jobs filter (line 141); with a selective filter most 1000-event batches return empty while done stays false, so the loop sleeps 20ms per batch of a file that is fully readable. The IDLE_DELAY comment ('A source that streams (a log) never idles ... so it pays no sleep') documents that this was not intended.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath replay bigrun.jsonl <one-job-id>` on a 5M-event log: ~5000 empty filtered batches each pay a 0.02s sleep, adding ~100 seconds of pure sleeping to a replay that should take a few seconds; the terminal appears to trickle/hang between the selected job's events.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Distinguish 'source produced nothing' from 'everything was filtered': have JSONLFileProducer expose idle (raw batch empty) like LiveProducer does, or have RenderLoop consult $producer->idle when available instead of the returned event count.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor addition: even an unfiltered replay pays one stray 20ms sleep when a batch consists solely of the harness_final event (it is captured, not returned, so @out is empty while done is still false) — negligible, but it shows IDLE is keyed to "events returned" rather than "source exhausted" generally. Fix as proposed: have JSONLFileProducer expose idle => raw-batch-empty (like LiveProducer) and have RenderLoop prefer $producer->idle when the producer can('idle'), falling back to the returned-event count otherwise.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix: add an `idle` method to JSONLFileProducer (true only when the raw stream->poll batch is empty) and have RenderLoop::iterate use `$producer->can('idle') ? $producer->idle : !@events` — mirrors LiveProducer and matches the design intent documented at RenderLoop.pm:196-198. Also note poll() can return empty without a filter when a batch contains only the captured harness_final event, a second (rarer) instance of the same miscounting. No existing TODO_TASKS.md item covers this.

acc_verdict.reason: Confirmed by tracing the full path. Command/replay.pm:61-78 builds a jobs filter from extra CLI args and drives the loop via $loop->start. JSONLFileProducer::poll (lib/App/Yath2/RenderLoop/JSONLFileProducer.pm:114-147) sets DONE only when the RAW stream batch is empty (line 118-121), but returns only post-filter events (line 141 drops non-matching job_ids, lines 136-139 also withhold harness_final). RenderLoop::iterate (lib/App/Yath2/RenderLoop.pm:221) computes IDLE from that post-filter count, and start (line 206) sleeps 0.02s whenever IDLE and not done. So every 1000-event batch fully consumed by the filter costs a 20ms sleep on a file that is immediately readable; nothing resets IDLE between poll and sleep, and JSONLFileProducer has no idle method for the loop to consult (only LiveProducer does, LiveProducer.pm:20). The IDLE_DELAY comment (RenderLoop.pm:196-198, "A source that streams (a log) never idles ... so it pays no sleep") documents that log replay was intended to pay no sleep, so this is unintended, not by-design. The ~100s estimate for a 5M-event log with a one-job filter (~5000 empty batches x 0.02s) is arithmetically sound.

Fix as proposed: have JSONLFileProducer expose idle => raw-batch-empty (like LiveProducer) and have RenderLoop prefer $producer->idle when the producer can('idle'), falling back to the returned-event count otherwise.

confirmedFindings.title: Composer render_info/render_errors compute a dumped $msg for ref details but emit the raw ref, rendering as HASH(0x...)
confirmedFindings.evidence: In both files, render_info builds `$msg` via Data::Dumper when `ref($details)` (lines 279-286) but then returns `['info', $_->{tag}, $details, ...]` (line 288) — $msg is dead. render_errors does the same (`['error', $tag, $details]` at line 328). The formatter's build_line then does `split /[\r\n]/, $text` on the ref, stringifying it. (Same dead code exists in reference/pre_ai_2.0, but the computed-then-discarded $msg makes the intent unambiguous.)
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A test emits an error or info facet whose details is a data structure (e.g. an exception object serialized to a hash in facet_data, common for structured error facets). Instead of the dumped structure, the terminal line reads '<  ERROR  >  HASH(0x55f3a2c41d80)', hiding the actual error content from the user.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Emit $msg instead of $details in the returned tuples: ['info', $_->{tag}, $msg, $_->{table} || ()] and ['error', $tag, $msg].
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two precision notes: (1) this is not a 2.0 rewrite regression — the identical dead $msg exists in reference/legacy (shipped CPAN 1.x Test2::Formatter::Test2::Composer) and reference/pre_ai_2.0, so it is a long-standing inherited upstream bug, supporting the P3 severity; (2) the App::Yath2::Renderer::Default::Composer copy is currently referenced by nothing else under lib/ (Test2::Formatter::Test2 uses its own Composer), so the only live terminal-output impact today is via lib/Test2/Formatter/Test2/Composer.pm — fix both to keep the copies in sync. The proposal (emit $msg in both tuples) is correct.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Trivial fix: return $msg instead of $details in both tuples (render_info line 288, render_errors line 328) in both lib/App/Yath2/Renderer/Default/Composer.pm and lib/Test2/Formatter/Test2/Composer.pm; worth fixing in passing during any Composer/renderer chunk (e.g. remaining render-loop follow-ups), and upstreaming to the 1.x maint branch since the same dead code is in the released CPAN dist. No matching entry found needed in TODO_TASKS.md; a one-line note there would suffice.

acc_verdict.reason: Traced end to end and confirmed. In both Composer copies (lines 271-330), render_info and render_errors compute a Data::Dumper $msg for ref($details) (lines 278-286 / 316-324) but return $details in the tuple (lines 288 / 328); $msg is dead. confirmedFindings.title: Jsonl renderer never checks print/close results — a failed log write still reports 'Wrote log file'
confirmedFindings.evidence: render_event's `print $fh $event->as_json` return is ignored, and finish() does `print $fh "null\n"; close($fh);` with no check on either (close is where buffered/compressed data is flushed — ENOSPC/EIO surfaces there for IO::Compress handles and buffered writes). finish() then unconditionally prints 'Wrote log file: ...' as a success message.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Disk fills mid-run while logging with -L: events are silently dropped from the .jsonl, close() fails to flush the compressed tail (truncated .gz/.bz2), yet yath prints 'Wrote log file: run.jsonl.gz' with exit 0 for a passing suite; the user later discovers the archived log is truncated/corrupt with no warning ever issued.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Check close($fh) (and optionally accumulate print failures) in finish(); on failure warn and skip the 'Wrote log file' success message (or die so the run is marked unhealthy).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Line anchors per the finding's accuracy_note are correct: unchecked print at 107 (render_event), unchecked print/close at 118-119 (finish), unconditional success message at 125-127. One added nuance: on the plain uncompressed path the handle is buffered stdio, so per-event print failures typically surface only at close — meaning the proposed `close($fh) or warn/skip-success` check in finish is the primary fix for BOTH compressed and plain paths, with per-event print checks as optional hardening. Severity sits at the P2/P3 boundary: it needs an environmental fault (disk full/IO error) and does not affect test results or exit status, but a falsely-blessed corrupt -L archive loses the run's only record, so P2 is kept.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix, as the finding's own severity_note observes: this rides on existing TODO_TASKS.md #55/#56 (DB-Jsonl step) which already own this renderer. Minimal patch: `close($fh) or do { warn "Failed writing log '$self->{+FILE}': $!"; return }` inserted before the success-message block in finish() (after the `print $fh "null\n"` line), since IO::Compress handles surface flush/trailer errors specifically via close() — checking close() alone catches the dominant failure mode (ENOSPC/EIO/compressed-tail corruption) without needing per-print checks, which are optional hardening only. No architectural change needed; safe to fold into the existing #55/#56 pass over this file.

confirmedFindings.title: find_multi_project_files: unchecked chdir($pdir) silently scans the wrong directory
confirmedFindings.evidence: Line 543: `chdir($pdir) if defined $pdir;` — the return value is not checked, unlike the per-project `chdir($path) or die "Could not chdir to $path: $!\n";` nine lines later (line 554). On failure the code proceeds with `my $ret = clean_path(getcwd());` — i.e. the unchanged current directory — and enumerates its subdirectories as "projects".
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath projects /no/such/dir` (typo'd or deleted project dir, or a dir without execute permission): chdir fails silently, yath treats every subdirectory of the CURRENT working directory as a project, discovers and runs whatever t/ dirs those happen to contain (or dies with a confusing 'No tests to run' from the wrong tree). The user gets a test run of the wrong code — possibly a passing one — instead of an error naming the bad path.
confirmedFindings.proposal: `chdir($pdir) or die "Could not chdir to '$pdir': $!\n" if defined $pdir;`
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Finding is accurate as written. Minor additions: the same sub also has two other unchecked chdir calls (`chdir($ret)` at lines 548 and 562), which are lower risk since $ret was just a successful getcwd, and the eval/restore at lines 565-567 restores the original dir either way. The proposed one-line fix is correct; note Perl parsing requires parens or restructuring: `if (defined $pdir) { chdir($pdir) or die "Could not chdir to '$pdir': $!\n" }` rather than `... or die ... if defined $pdir;` (the latter actually parses fine too, but the block form is clearer).

confirmedFindings.title: APP_PATH computed with greedy regex strips too much when path contains an earlier 'App'
confirmedFindings.evidence: `$APP_PATH =~ s{App\S+Yath2\.pm$}{}g;` — `\S+` is greedy and unanchored on the left, so the match starts at the FIRST 'App' substring in the path. Verified: '/home/u/Apps/x/lib/App/Yath2.pm' becomes '/home/u/' instead of '/home/u/Apps/x/lib/'. Any 'App' occurring earlier in the checkout path (Apps, AppData, MyApp, Application...) triggers it.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A user whose checkout lives under e.g. ~/Apps/ or ~/Application/ runs the test suite: App::Yath2->app_path returns a truncated directory, so App::Yath2::Tester pushes a wrong `-D$apppath`/`-I$apppath` (lines 164-166 of Tester.pm) into every nested yath invocation. The nested yath silently loads the installed Test2-Harness libraries instead of the dev checkout — tests exercise the wrong code and pass/fail misleadingly.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Replace with a non-greedy/anchored strip, e.g. `$APP_PATH =~ s{App[/\\]+Yath2\.pm$}{};` (and drop the useless /g).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Trigger requires __FILE__ to be an absolute path with an earlier 'App' substring (absolute -I/-D/PERL5LIB load; a relative -Ilib load gives __FILE__='lib/App/Yath2.pm' and is unaffected). If Test2-Harness is not also installed system-wide, the nested yath fails loudly (module not found) rather than silently testing the wrong code; the silent-wrong-code scenario needs an installed copy present.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix (apply in passing): in lib/App/Yath2.pm:33 replace `$APP_PATH =~ s{App\S+Yath2\.pm$}{}g;` with an anchored component match `$APP_PATH =~ s{App[/\\]+Yath2\.pm$}{};` (the /g is useless due to $ anchor), or more robustly `File::Basename::dirname(dirname(__FILE__))`. confirmedFindings.title: .yath.rc section header with trailing whitespace or trailing comment is silently parsed as an option/argument
confirmedFindings.evidence: Line 101 matches the section header (`m/^\[(.*)\]$/`, anchored at end-of-line) BEFORE the comment strip (line 102 `s/;.*$//g`) and whitespace trim (lines 103-104). So a line `[test] ` (trailing space) or `[test] ; my note` — the documented comment syntax per the App::Yath2 POD ('Comments start with a semi-colon') — fails the anchored match, then gets trimmed and pushed into %CONFIG as the literal argument '[test]' under the wrong section. (Bonus: `$cmd = $1 and next` also fails to `next` for a section literally named `[0]`.)
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User writes `[test] ;always log` (or leaves a trailing space after `[test]`) in .yath.rc. The '[test]' token flows through stage-1 parsing as a non-option: with `yath` (no explicit command) it becomes the fallback command and yath dies "yath command '[test]' not found"; with `yath test` it rides into the final argv and the finder dies "'[test]' is not a valid file or directory." — a cryptic failure caused by invisible whitespace, and the options meant for that section bind to the previous/global section.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Strip comments/whitespace first, then match the section header: move lines 102-104 above line 101, or relax the regex to `m/^\[(.*?)\]\s*$/` and use `if (...) { $cmd = $1; next; }`.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Scenario and lines are precise as written. Minor addition: the misparse also silently rebinds every option under the malformed header to the previous/global section, which can change test-run behavior (e.g. a [start] option applied globally) even when the literal '[test]' token happens to be consumed without a fatal error. Fix both bugs at once: replace V2.pm:101 with `if ($line =~ m/^\[(.*?)\]\s*(?:;.*)?$/) { $cmd = $1; next; }`.

sev_verdict.reason:
Trigger is real and reachable in any supported config: a .yath.rc section header with trailing whitespace or an inline ';' comment (documented comment syntax) is misparsed as a literal argument, causing a cryptic startup die and section options binding to the wrong section. However, it requires that specific rc-file formatting, fails fast and loudly in most cases, and the identical code has shipped in legacy 1.x (reference/legacy/lib/App/Yath/Script/V1.pm:39) for years without apparent field reports — an edge case needing unusual conditions, not a common-path failure.</parameter>

confirmedFindings.title: Tester yath() timeout recovery blocks forever: TERM then waitpid(pid,0) with no KILL escalation
confirmedFindings.evidence: On timeout: `kill('TERM', $pid); waitpid($pid, 0);` — a blocking wait with no deadline and no SIGKILL fallback. The child is a full yath run whose transient client traps TERM (App::Yath2::Client::handle_signal forwards the signal to the runner and keeps waiting for the runner to tear down); if the run is wedged — which is exactly the situation that made the timeout fire — TERM does not guarantee exit.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A yath child spawned by yath() wedges (e.g. runner deadlock, a test child ignoring TERM keeping the collector alive). After YATH_TESTER_TIMEOUT (120s) the tester sends TERM; the yath process catches it, forwards it, and continues waiting on its wedged runner. waitpid(pid,0) then never returns, so the 'timeout' converts into an infinite hang of the calling test file — the timeout mechanism defeats itself.
confirmedFindings.proposal: After TERM, poll with WNOHANG for a grace period (a few seconds), then `kill('KILL', $pid)` (ideally the process group) before the final blocking waitpid.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Fix at lib/App/Yath2/Tester.pm:210: after kill('TERM',$pid), poll waitpid($pid,WNOHANG) with Time::HiRes::sleep for a ~5s grace, then kill('KILL',$pid) followed by a blocking waitpid. Because run_cmd uses no_set_pgrp=>1, KILL-to-pid may orphan grandchildren (the runner/collector tree); consider dropping no_set_pgrp or recording the child pgid so kill(-$pgid) can sweep the tree. Note Client's escalation path (second-signal exit) exists but Tester sends only one TERM; alternatively sending a second TERM after the grace would also trip Client's exit-now branch, but KILL is the robust choice since the runner itself may be unkillable-by-TERM.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix at lib/App/Yath2/Tester.pm:210: after kill('TERM',$pid), loop waitpid($pid,WNOHANG) with Time::HiRes::sleep for a ~5s grace, then kill('KILL',$pid) and blocking waitpid. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this.

confirmedFindings.title: Discovery->find unlinks the symlink on any connect failure, destroying the documented PID-file fallback for a wedged runner
confirmedFindings.evidence: find() (lines 159-162) calls resolves(), and on ANY connect failure calls $self->clean, which unlinks the symlink unconditionally (no errno classification, no ownership check). But the module's own contract (lines 40-44, 89-92, 240-244) says the workdir PID file — reachable ONLY via this symlink — exists precisely 'for signalling a wedged runner whose socket no longer accepts or responds'. probe()/list() carefully distinguish EACCES/EPERM ('inaccessible', never cleaned) and clean only via clean_if_owned; find() does neither. Pfile->find (the path used by stop/which/kill) wraps find().
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A persistent runner wedges with its listen socket closed (or its socket becomes unreadable): the process is still alive, still holding resources and respawning preload stages. The user runs `yath stop` (or `yath which`): Pfile->find → Discovery->find gets a connect failure, deletes the discovery symlink, and returns nothing. yath reports no persistent harness found; the only pointer to the workdir/PID file is now gone, so the documented signal-based termination fallback is impossible — the wedged runner is orphaned until the user hunts the pid by hand.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In find(), classify the failure like probe() does: only clean on a dangling link / missing target / ECONNREFUSED, and even then via clean_if_owned; on other connect errors return a discovery object flagged not-live so commands like stop can still reach the workdir PID file.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two precision corrections to the scenario: (1) a merely-hung runner whose listener fd is still open passes resolves() via the kernel accept backlog, so the destructive clean fires only when the listener is actually gone (partial crash / close-during-wedged-teardown per Runner.pm:516), the backlog has filled (EAGAIN), or the connect fails client-side (EMFILE, EACCES on another user's socket — healthy-runner cases); (2) stop/kill today drive teardown through the socket client (stop.pm:56-72, kill.pm:37-48) and have no implemented signal-only command path, so the immediate loss is discoverability (symlink deleted, wedged runner orphaned, later `yath run` silently sees no persistent harness) rather than breakage of an existing fallback command. Fix as proposed: make find() classify via probe() and clean only on state 'dead' using clean_if_owned; optionally return a not-live discovery object so stop can reach the workdir PID file. Folds into TODO_TASKS.md #95/#62.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix: make find() reuse probe() and clean only on state eq 'dead' (dangling link / missing target / ECONNREFUSED), via clean_if_owned instead of clean; optionally return a not-live discovery object so stop can still reach the workdir PID file. This folds naturally into existing tickets TODO_TASKS.md #95 (Pfile shim removal — migrates every affected call site to Discovery) or #62 (REF-PORT list/ping — already adds Discovery->list and reworks persist commands); sequencing notes at TODO_TASKS.md:1611 already order #95 before #62. Fixing the clean/clean_if_owned asymmetry also closes the minor multi-user hole (find can unlink another user's link where directory perms allow, unlike list).

sev_verdict.reason: The trigger is real but requires unusual state: a truly hung runner still passes resolves() via the kernel listen backlog, so the destructive clean fires only when the listener fd is gone while the socket file remains (partial daemon crash / fd exhaustion) or when the client-side connect fails transiently (connect_unix is eval-wrapped, so client EMFILE or EACCES on another user's socket also counts — in that case find() unlinks the link for a HEALTHY runner, and clean() skips the ownership check clean_if_owned enforces). All Pfile consumers (stop/kill/which/status/ps/run/resources) reach this path with no no_clean. Impact when hit is user-visible but bounded: the discovery symlink (sole pointer to workdir/PID) is deleted, yath reports no persistent harness, and the wedged daemon is orphaned until the user hunts the pid by hand; workdir+PID file still exist on disk, and notably stop/kill today drive teardown through the socket client anyway (kill.pm:37-46, stop.pm:46-72), so the documented signal-only fallback is not currently an implemented command path — the loss is discoverability plus, in the transient-client-failure case, a later `yath run` silently treating the persistent runner as absent. confirmedFindings.title: .yath.rc glob()/relglob() shells out with unquoted interpolation; quotes/spaces in paths silently drop config values
confirmedFindings.evidence: Line 150: ``my $out = `$^X -e 'print join "\\n" => glob("${path}${val}")'`;`` — $path (derived from the rc-file path, i.e. the project checkout location) and $val are interpolated raw into a single-quoted shell word and a double-quoted Perl string. A single quote in the path breaks the shell command; a double quote breaks the -e program; a space makes Perl's csh-style glob() treat the path as two patterns. Backtick failure is unchecked: @vals ends up empty and @all becomes an empty list, so the config option vanishes without any diagnostic.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A project at /home/o'brien/proj (or any path with a space, e.g. under a mounted 'My Drive') uses `--default-search relglob(subprojects/*/t)` in .yath.rc: the subshell dies with a shell syntax error (swallowed), the option is silently dropped, and yath runs with the default t/ search instead of the configured one — wrong test set with zero indication why.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Pass path/pattern as argv (`$out = do { local $"; open my $p, '-|', $^X, '-e', 'print join "\n", glob($ARGV[0])', "${path}${val}" ... }`) or use bsd_glob in-process; at minimum check `$?` after the backticks and warn when the glob subprocess failed.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor correction: in the single-quote case the failure is not 100% silent — /bin/sh emits a syntax error on stderr (backticks capture stdout only), though it is cryptic and unattributed. The space and double-quote cases produce no diagnostic at all, and in every case the option drop itself is silent. Everything else (lines 138-153, mechanism, proposal, P3 severity) is accurate; the fix should use the multi-arg '-|' open (or in-process File::Glob::bsd_glob) and check child exit status.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix in passing: replace the backtick with list-form pipe-open (open my $p, '-|', $^X, '-e', 'print join "\n", glob($ARGV[0])', "${path}${val}") which removes the shell entirely and fixes quote/metachar breakage, and check close/$? to warn instead of silently dropping the option. Note the space case is only partially fixable this way: Perl's csh-style glob() splits patterns on whitespace regardless of how it is invoked, so a path with a space also needs the pattern wrapped as glob(qq{"$pat"}) or File::Glob::bsd_glob. The 'avoid loading File::Glob' comment is the only reason for the subprocess; if that constraint is no longer real, bsd_glob in-process is the simplest complete fix. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this (the only V2.pm item, line 2074, is about the stale 'V1 Legacy' POD, which could be corrected in the same commit).

acc_verdict.reason: Verified end to end. lib/App/Yath/Script/V2.pm:150 interpolates $path (directory of the .yath.rc file, i.e. the project location, per lines 143-147) and $val raw into `$^X -e '...glob("${path}${val}")'` backticks. A single quote in the path breaks the shell quoting; a double quote/$/@ breaks the child Perl one-liner; a space makes csh-style glob() split the pattern. Backtick status is never checked ($? is even explicitly reset to 0 at line 77 of setup()), so @vals/@all end up empty and the loop at line 158 runs zero times: the config option silently vanishes. No guard, sanitization, or test covers such paths (t/yath_script.t uses clean paths only). The shell-out itself is intentional (comment line 149: avoid loading File::Glob), but the quoting fragility and unchecked failure are real defects.

Everything else (lines 138-153, mechanism, proposal, P3 severity) is accurate; the fix should use the multi-arg '-|' open (or in-process File::Glob::bsd_glob) and check child exit status.

confirmedFindings.title: yath start deletes a LIVE runner's workdir when the workdir is reused and a runner is already running
confirmedFindings.evidence: start.pm run(): `my $dir = $settings->workspace->workdir; ... if (App::Yath2::Discovery->find($settings)) { remove_tree($dir, {safe => 1, keep_root => 0}); die "Persistent harness appears to be running..." }`. Options::Workspace lets the user pin the workdir via `-w`/`T2_WORKDIR`/`YATH_WORKDIR` (option_post_process only mkdirs it if missing; an existing dir is kept as-is). When the pinned dir IS the running runner's workdir, $dir contains the live runner's runner.socket, PID, settings.json and preload sockets, and remove_tree deletes them all before dying. The intent was clearly to clean up the freshly-created temp workdir of THIS aborted start attempt, but nothing checks that $dir is not the live runner's own dir.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `YATH_WORKDIR=/tmp/ydir yath start -Pfoo` (runner boots in /tmp/ydir), later re-runs the same command (shell history / a wrapper script with the env var set). Second start finds the live runner via the discovery symlink, then remove_tree('/tmp/ydir') unlinks the live runner's runner.socket, PID file and settings.json before printing 'Persistent harness appears to be running'. The discovery symlink now dangles, so the next `yath run`/`yath stop`/`yath which` cleans the link and reports no runner — the still-running runner daemon is orphaned (unstoppable except by manual kill) and every client connect fails.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Only remove_tree($dir) when $dir was freshly created for this invocation (e.g. skip when the workdir option came from the user/env, or compare $dir against the found discovery's workdir and never delete it when they match or when the dir already contains runner.socket/PID).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Slightly broader than stated: the unguarded remove_tree deletes ANY user-pinned workdir on this abort path, not only when it equals the live runner's workdir — e.g. runner started with a default tempdir workdir, then `yath -w ~/some-existing-dir start` wipes ~/some-existing-dir before dying. The pinned-dir==runner-dir case is the worst instance (orphans the daemon); the general fix should be as proposed: only remove_tree when the dir was freshly created for this invocation (or never when it contains runner.socket/PID or matches the found discovery's workdir). Anchor lines: start.pm:131 ($dir resolved) and start.pm:142 (remove_tree).
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix: skip remove_tree when $dir contains runner.socket/PID, or when the discovery link's resolved socket path is inside $dir, or only clean when Workspace.pm generated the tempdir this invocation (record a created-this-run flag in option_post_process). Could be folded into TODO_TASKS.md #51 (runner workdir-cleanup deferral / vanished-workdir detection, line ~1247), which already touches workdir lifecycle. Note clear_env_vars on the workdir option strips the pin from child env but does nothing for sibling invocations from the same shell.

acc_verdict.reason: Traced end to end and confirmed. Options::Workspace lets -w/T2_WORKDIR/YATH_WORKDIR pin the workdir, and option_post_process keeps an existing dir untouched (Workspace.pm:116-129), so on a repeated `YATH_WORKDIR=/tmp/ydir yath start -Pfoo` the second invocation's $dir IS the live runner's workdir. start.pm:141-143 then finds the live runner via Discovery->find (symlink resolves to /tmp/ydir/runner.socket, -S passes, connect_unix succeeds) and unconditionally remove_tree($dir, keep_root=>0) before dying — deleting the live runner's runner.socket, PID file, settings.json and preload sockets (safe=>1 does not protect same-owner files). confirmedFindings.title: Ctrl-C on `yath run` (attach mode) is completely unhandled: command dies mid-render, submitted run keeps executing on the persistent runner, renderers/log never flushed
confirmedFindings.evidence: run.pm sets `sub client_mode { 'attach' }`. test.pm start() calls $self->install_signal_handlers() which delegates to App::Yath2::Client::install_signal_handlers, whose first line is `return unless $self->{+MODE} eq MODE_TRANSIENT;` (Client.pm:210) — so for the persistent `yath run` path NO INT/HUP/TERM handlers are ever installed (verified: no other $SIG{INT} installer exists on this path). All the signal machinery run.pm inherits from test.pm (stop()'s `signal_shutdown`/halt_run, 'Waiting for child processes...', renderer ->signal relay) is dead code in attach mode. Legacy 1.x run.pm inherited test.pm's Test2::Harness::IPC INT/TERM handlers, so this is a behavior regression, not a port of old behavior.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath run t/` against a persistent runner and presses Ctrl-C. Default SIGINT kills the command instantly: (1) halt_run is never sent, so the whole submitted run keeps executing to completion inside the persistent runner, silently consuming CPU and serializing behind-the-scenes with the user's next `yath run`; (2) renderer finish() never runs — a `-F log.jsonl` file is left without its `null` terminator and 'Wrote log file' never prints, and the ResetTerm renderer's terminal reset never fires (END blocks do not run on default-signal death), leaving a live status bar garbling the terminal; (3) spawned -L DB loggers in the same process group also die mid-import.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Install INT/HUP/TERM handlers for attach mode too (set the signal flag, stop the render loop, send halt_run for this run_id over runner.socket, finish renderers), reusing the existing signal_shutdown path that is currently unreachable.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Correct the failure scenario: on Ctrl-C the run IS aborted runner-side via the owner-disconnect sweep (Handlers.pm service_conn_closed -> handle_owner_drop, abort_on_disconnect default true), so drop claim (1) entirely. The real defect is client-side ungraceful death only: (a) ResetTerm's reset (END block + finish()) never runs, leaving the status bar's terminal state dirty; (b) a -F log.jsonl is left without its null terminator and 'Wrote log file' never prints; (c) client-spawned -L DB loggers in the foreground process group die mid-import (though the runner's SUBSCRIBER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT bounds the workdir-cleanup wait); (d) all of test.pm's signal machinery (signal_shutdown, 'Waiting for child processes...') is dead code in attach mode. Proposal stands but simplify: install INT/HUP/TERM handlers in attach mode that set the signal flag and stop the render loop so stop() flushes renderers; sending halt_run is still worthwhile for promptness/explicitness but is not required to stop the run (disconnect already aborts it). Keep the second-Ctrl-C hard-exit convention.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix reusing existing machinery: drop the MODE_TRANSIENT early-return in Client::install_signal_handlers and make handle_signal mode-aware — in attach mode set the signal flag and send a halt_run/stop request for this run_id over runner.socket instead of signaling the runner's process group; test.pm's existing post-loop `signal_shutdown` (test.pm:475/501) then flushes renderers/log for free (it is currently dead code in attach mode). No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this specifically; the chunk-21 client/mode-enum entry (~line 923) is the natural place to fold it in. Sub-issue worth noting for the fixer: a second Ctrl-C should still hard-exit (transient handle_signal already has that convention).

sev_verdict.reason: Trigger is trivially reachable in normal use: Ctrl-C during `yath run` against a persistent runner is a routine interactive-dev action, and the code chain is confirmed (run.pm client_mode 'attach'; test.pm:193 -> Client.pm install_signal_handlers bails at line 210 `return unless $self->{+MODE} eq MODE_TRANSIENT`; no other INT/HUP/TERM installer exists on this path). No hang/deadlock and the daemon itself stays healthy, so not P0; but far more than an edge case, and a regression vs legacy 1.x which did install handlers here — P1.

confirmedFindings.title: `yath start --daemon` prints 'Persistent runner started!' and exits 0 without any liveness check — a runner that dies during boot yields a false success (after a possible silent 30s stall)
confirmedFindings.evidence: run() spawns the runner (start_runner), publishes the discovery symlink unconditionally, then wait_for_runner_pid() polls only for the $dir/PID FILE (600 x 0.05s), falling back silently to the collector-parent pid (`// $pid`). Nothing ever verifies the runner process is alive or that runner.socket bound before printing the banner and `return 0 if $settings->runner->daemon;`. The daemon collector's stdout/stderr are detached to /dev/null (per the client() comment), so a boot crash produces no visible output. Runner.pm writes PID (line 439) before preloads load, so a bad -P preload crashes AFTER the PID file appears — the banner prints immediately with a dead pid.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath start -d -PBroken::Module && yath run t/` in a script: the runner execs, writes PID, then dies loading the broken preload with its error swallowed into runner-events under a detached daemon. `yath start` prints 'Persistent runner started! / Runner PID: <dead pid>' and exits 0, so the && proceeds; `yath run` then dies with 'No persistent harness was found for the current path.' with no hint why. In the variant where the runner dies before writing PID, the user additionally sits through a silent 30-second wait_for_runner_pid stall before the false success banner.
confirmedFindings.proposal: After publish, verify liveness before the banner: kill(0, $pid) / waitpid WNOHANG on the collector child, plus a bounded wait for the discovery symlink to resolve to an accepting runner.socket (Discovery->resolves). Print a failure message and exit non-zero if the runner never comes up.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One strengthening detail: the runner's death on a broken preload is not merely a crash that gets 'swallowed' -- it is an explicit fail-fast/terminate path in Runner.pm (~1184-1192, stage_host_exited / _handle_dead_preload_root), so the runner reliably exits after writing PID, making the false-success banner deterministic for any bad -P module, not just a lucky race. Also note the contrast within the same function: the foreground (--no-daemon) branch at start.pm:183-196 waits and propagates the runner exit code, so the daemon branch's missing liveness check is an inconsistency, not a design choice.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap mitigation: after wait_for_runner_pid, do a bounded kill(0, $runner_pid) liveness check (and/or waitpid WNOHANG on the collector child $pid to see if it already reaped with an error) before printing the success banner and returning 0; if dead, print a failure and propagate a non-zero exit. Could also treat a successful connect to $dir/runner.socket as the actual readiness signal instead of relying on the PID file alone, reusing existing Discovery->resolves machinery. No existing TODO_TASKS.md item found covering this specific daemon-liveness gap.

confirmedFindings.title: spawn.pm resets %SIG with a NUMERIC signal from parse_exit, emitting a 'No such signal: SIG15' warning and never actually resetting the named handler
confirmedFindings.evidence: run(): `if ($exit->{sig}) { print STDERR "Terminated with signal: $exit->{sig}.\n"; $SIG{$exit->{sig}} = 'DEFAULT'; kill($exit->{sig}, $$); }`. parse_exit() (Test2::Harness2::Util:199) returns sig as a NUMBER (`$exit & 127`). %SIG keys must be signal NAMES: empirically `$SIG{15} = 'DEFAULT'` warns 'No such signal: SIG15' and does not touch the SIGTERM handler. The re-raise still works only because _clear_sig_forwarding() happened to reset the forwarded set by name earlier; the message also reports a bare number instead of a name.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath spawn script.pl`, then the spawned child is killed with SIGTERM. The command prints 'Terminated with signal: 15.' followed by the spurious warning 'No such signal: SIG15 at .../spawn.pm line 255.' on the user's terminal before re-killing itself. Were sig_handlers ever extended (or the ordering changed) so a forwarded handler was still installed, the reset would silently fail and kill() would re-enter the forwarding handler instead of terminating.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Convert the number to a name via Config's sig_name (e.g. `my @names = split ' ', $Config{sig_name}; my $name = $names[$exit->{sig}]`) and use the name for both the message and the %SIG reset.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor precision: the warning fires under spawn.pm's file-scoped `use warnings` (not only under -w), and kill() itself accepts numeric signals fine — the defect is confined to the %SIG reset (silent no-op with a warning) and the numeric signal in the user-facing message. Today's user-visible impact is exactly one spurious 'No such signal: SIG15' warning line on STDERR per signal-terminated spawn plus the numeric message; the failed handler reset is latent because _clear_sig_forwarding() has already restored DEFAULT for every signal in sig_handlers before line 255 runs.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Upgrading from the pre-existing P3 to P2: not merely theoretical — the warning line reliably prints to the user's terminal on any normal signal-terminated `yath spawn` (Ctrl-C, external kill), which is common in interactive/CI use, so it's more than "unusual conditions." But it stays out of P1 because exit code/results are unaffected in the current code path (the effective reset already happened by name in _clear_sig_forwarding before this redundant numeric one runs) — it's cosmetic stderr noise, not observably wrong behavior. Cheap mitigation matches the finding's own proposal: resolve the number to a name via `%Config::Config` `sig_name` (or simply drop the now-redundant reset entirely, since _clear_sig_forwarding already covers it by name) and use the name in both the message and any %SIG write. No related TODO_TASKS.md entry found for this specific spot.

confirmedFindings.title: -L DB loggers are silently SIGTERM'd after the 120s teardown timeout and their exit status is never checked, so an incomplete/failed DB import goes unreported
confirmedFindings.evidence: wait_for_loggers(): after the 120s WNOHANG poll loop, `for my $pid (@left) { kill('TERM', $pid); }` — no message is printed to the user, the killed pids are never reaped (zombies until process exit), and for loggers that DO exit within the window the waitpid status ($?) is discarded, so a logger that exited non-zero (DB unreachable, import error, or the exec-127 failure path of run_cmd's child) is indistinguishable from success. start_loggers() likewise never validates the logger came up. The bounded wait itself is deliberate (per the comment), but the silence is not: the command exits with its normal pass/fail status implying the -L target was written.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath test -L<db-target> t/` on a large suite where the DB import legitimately needs more than 120 seconds (slow remote DB). After the tests pass, wait_for_loggers TERMs the logger mid-import and yath exits 0 printing nothing about it; the user's database silently contains a truncated run. Same silent outcome if the logger died at startup with a bad DSN: the run completes, exit 0, no DB rows, no warning.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Print a warning naming the pids when the timeout fires ('DB logger <pid> did not finish within 120s; import may be incomplete'), reap after TERM, and check the waitpid status of cleanly-exited loggers, warning on non-zero exits.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One sub-claim is overstated: the bad-DSN/startup-failure case is not fully silent at the terminal. start_loggers passes no stdout/stderr redirects to run_cmd, so the logger inherits the terminal STDERR, and Logger::_record_error does `warn "DB logger: $msg\n"` before the process exits 1 (Logger.pm 678-688); the exec-127 path also prints to the cloned STDERR (IPC.pm 131-140). What is missing there is harness-level reporting and any exit-status effect, not all output. The zombie claim is technically true but trivial: wait_for_loggers runs at the tail of stop() and the command exits moments later. The truly silent data-loss case is exactly the timeout-TERM mid-import path, which additionally leaves runs.status='running' in the DB (no 'broken' marker) since _finalize_run_row never runs after SIGTERM.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this specific gap (the #50 DB-logger design ticket covers spawning/lifecycle but not swallowing exit status or the timeout being silent). Cheap fix matches the finding's proposal and is genuinely cheap: on timeout, print one warning naming the still-running pids before TERM; after TERM, waitpid (blocking, since they were just signalled) to reap instead of leaving zombies; for loggers that exited within the window, check $? and warn on non-zero. None of this needs new plumbing -- $self already has access to the command's normal warn/print channel used elsewhere in test.pm.

confirmedFindings.title: yath failed crashes with 'Modification of non-creatable array value' on logs where a failing job has no harness_job_end
confirmedFindings.evidence: Line 69 creates $failed{$job_id} whenever a top-level failing subtest event is seen (push @{$failed{$job_id}->{subtests}}), independent of any harness_job_end. Lines 87/90 then unconditionally deref $ends->[-1] where $ends = $data->{ends} // []. If no harness_job_end event exists for that job, @$ends is empty and $ends->[-1]->{rel_file} / $ends->[-1]->{fail} is a chained deref that tries to autovivify index -1 of an empty array. Verified experimentally: perl -Mstrict -we 'my $ends=[]; $ends->[-1]->{rel_file}' dies with "Modification of non-creatable array value attempted, subscript -1".
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath failed run.jsonl` (or `--brief`) on a log from an interrupted/aborted run (Ctrl-C, yath abort, crashed collector) where a test emitted a failing top-level subtest event but the run ended before its harness_job_end was written. The command dies mid-report with "Modification of non-creatable array value attempted, subscript -1" instead of listing the failures — exactly the aborted-run case where the user most wants the failure list.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Guard the deref: `my $end = @$ends ? $ends->[-1] : undef;` and render 'N/A'/unknown rel_file with 'Times Run' 0 when $end is undef (or skip such jobs with a note), in both the brief and table branches.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor precision: in the --brief branch the die occurs while evaluating the `if` condition on line 87 itself (before any print), so even jobs that would print nothing crash the command. Otherwise the finding's lines, mechanism, and scenario are exact.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Upgrading from the finder's P2 to P1: `yath failed` is specifically the postmortem/diagnostic command users reach for after killing a hung or long failing run (Ctrl-C, CI job cancellation, OOM-killed worker) -- exactly the scenario that produces a truncated log missing the final harness_job_end. That is a routine, not exotic, trigger path, and the failure mode is a hard crash of the one command meant to summarize failures, right when the user most needs it, so it fits "user-visible wrong behavior plausible in normal use" better than "edge case needing unusual conditions." Not P0 since there's no hang/spin/data loss -- the underlying JSONL log is untouched and a rerun of `yath failed` after the fix would work fine. Cheap fix, exactly as proposed: `my $end = @$ends ? $ends->[-1] : undef;` then guard both the brief-mode print and the table-row push on `defined $end` (rendering e.g. 'N/A'/unknown file otherwise). No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry covers this specific crash (nearby entries are about cli_args/doc_args and JSONL-scan duplication, not this deref bug), so it isn't already slated to be fixed in passing.

confirmedFindings.title: yath times: sorting by the 'file' field silently does nothing (looks up file in the times hash)
confirmedFindings.evidence: run() stores the file at $job->{file} and the times hash at $job->{time} (lines 83-84; the times hash contains only startup/events/cleanup/total). sort_compare (lines 128-133) resolves every field, including 'file', against $ta = $ja->{time}: `my $fa = $ta->{$field};` — so for field 'file' both sides are always undef and line 138 `next unless $da || $db` skips it. 'file' is an advertised sortable field (@ALPHA, line 37) and cli_args documents field arguments.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath times log.jsonl file` expecting file-name ordering. The 'file' comparison is always skipped, so output is actually sorted by the next appended field ('total'), i.e. the user's requested primary sort key is silently ignored. 'file' as a tiebreaker in the default order is likewise dead.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Special-case the file field in sort_compare: `my $fa = $field eq 'file' ? $ja->{file} : $ta->{$field};` (same for $fb).
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Trivially reachable (no unusual condition — just `yath times log.jsonl file`), so P3 slightly undersells it; bumping to P2 since it's a real, easily-triggered, user-visible defect, but capping there because it only mis-sorts a diagnostic report table and has zero effect on test execution/results/exit codes.
