Given the alias is undocumented anywhere and speedtag never self-generates the short form, I'd rate this P2 (edge case / unusual, non-standard input) rather than P1, contrary to nothing since the original audit already rated it P3 — bumping to P2 mainly because the bug is real, deterministic, and silently produces an incorrect scheduling decision rather than being purely cosmetic/latent.

confirmedFindings.title: Status-bar counters mishandle retries: a to-be-retried failure is counted in F permanently and the todo count goes negative
confirmedFindings.evidence: update_active_disp: harness_job_launch does `running++; todo--` with no retry awareness (line 383), and harness_job_end does `failed++` whenever end->{fail} is set (line 394) even when end->{retry} is set (the 'TO RETRY' attempt). A retried job sequence is: queued(T=1) -> launch(R=1,T=0) -> fail-with-retry end(F=1) -> relaunch(R=1, T=-1) -> pass end(P=1). No harness_job_queued is re-emitted for the retry (Base::render_run_start emits one per task, once).
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: TTY run with --retry: after a flaky test fails once and then passes, the status bar reads [P:1|F:1|R:0|T:-1] for the rest of the run — a failure count of 1 on a run that will be reported PASSED, and a nonsensical negative todo. Users watching the bar believe a test failed.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In update_active_disp, treat an end with {retry} as neither passed nor failed (increment a retry counter instead, and re-increment todo), or key launch on harness_job_launch->{retry} to skip the todo-- for re-launches.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two small corrections: (1) the end facet's {retry} flag is not produced by the collector/JobReader (JobReader hardcodes retry=>0); it is injected by Renderer::Base::note_verdict($end->{retry}=1 when tries remain) before the end event is dispatched, so the formatter does see it — the finding's evidence is right in effect but wrong about the flag's origin. (2) Both proposal options are viable: treating an end with {retry} as neither passed nor failed (re-incrementing todo), or skipping todo-- when harness_job_launch->{retry} is true (Driver::_render_launch passes retry=>$try at Driver.pm:336). Cited lines and scenario otherwise accurate; TTY-progress-only display defect, P3 stands.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: If/when this formatter is reintroduced as an active status-bar renderer (or if legacy bin/yath in reference/old2 or reference/legacy is still shipped/used by some users), this becomes P1/P2 (misleading pass/fail counts during --retry runs, visible in normal use). Cheap fix per the proposal: key off harness_job_end->{retry} to skip the failed++ and re-increment todo on relaunch, or track a separate retry bucket. No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry found for this specific counter bug.

confirmedFindings.title: Formatter DESTROY writes an ANSI reset escape to non-TTY / --no-color output
confirmedFindings.evidence: DESTROY prints `Term::ANSIColor::color('reset')` gated only on USE_ANSI_COLOR, which is purely 'Term::ANSIColor >= 4.03 is installed' (Test2/Harness2/Util/Term.pm) — it ignores both $self->{+COLOR} and TTY-ness. VERIFIED LIVE: `yath test --no-color file.t | head` (piped, non-TTY, color explicitly off) ends with a literal `\e[0m` line after the summary.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Any redirected/captured yath run (CI logs, `yath test > log 2>&1`, tester-captured output) gets a stray `\e[0m` appended, even with --no-color. Log scrapers/diff-based CI checks see the escape byte; the project's own Tester.pm output assertions must work around it.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Gate the DESTROY reset on `$self->{+COLOR}` (the instance's actual color decision) instead of the module-availability constant.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Scenario and lines are precise as written. The proposal is correct but could reuse the existing accessor: DESTROY should emit $self->{+COLOR}->{reset} only when $self->{+COLOR} is set (mirroring the reset() helper at line 610), rather than the module-availability constant USE_ANSI_COLOR.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Original P3 rating is right and should stand. Cheap fix: change `if USE_ANSI_COLOR` to `if $self->{+COLOR} && USE_ANSI_COLOR` at Test2.pm:772, mirroring the existing correct pattern at line 182 in the same file — trivial one-line change, no test-plan risk. Worth bundling with the already-ticketed cleanup at TODO_TASKS.md:1627 (same file, same area, redundant-if at 181-194) since an agent touching that region for the other cleanup will have the file open anyway.

confirmedFindings.title: yath ping exits 0 when the runner stops responding
confirmedFindings.evidence: In the ping loop, a failed round-trip prints "ping: no response from runner -- it may have stopped" and `last`s out of the loop (lines ~71-75 of the POD-stripped body; original around line 73), after which run() falls through to `print "\nStopped.\n"; return 0;`. A missing pfile returns 1, but a dead/unresponsive runner returns 0.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Scripted health check `yath ping && deploy_more_tests` : the runner has crashed mid-session, ping prints the 'no response' line, yet the command exits 0 and the caller proceeds as if the runner were healthy. Inconsistent with the exit-1 'no runner found' path.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Return a nonzero exit (e.g. 1) on the no-response break path; keep 0 only for user-initiated SIGINT stop.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Fix should distinguish the no-response break from the SIGINT break: the fall-through also prints "Stopped." after the failure line, which reads as a clean user stop. Return nonzero on the line-74 last path; keep 0 for the $stop (signal) paths at lines 59/65-68.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap fix matches the proposal: return 1 (or a distinct code) on the no-response `last` path, keep 0 for the `$stop`-triggered (SIGINT/TERM) exit. Trivial one-line change — add `return 1;` right after the print at line 73, before `last`, and skip the shared return by structuring as `if (!$reply) { ...; return 1; }`. No TODO_TASKS.md entry currently covers ping's exit code; note this for the next task-list pass. Original P3 in state.json appears too low given this is a live, easily-triggered path (not requiring unusual conditions) even though its practical blast radius is limited to external scripts that check `yath ping`'s exit status rather than its printed output.

confirmedFindings.title: Every daemon deadline/timeout uses wall-clock Time::HiRes::time (no monotonic clock anywhere in lib/), so a clock step or suspend/resume mass-fires or stalls them
confirmedFindings.evidence: grep for CLOCK_MONOTONIC/clock_gettime over lib/ returns nothing; every deadline is `time + N` / `time - $since > N` on wall clock: collector-connect-timeout (Handlers.pm:709-714, default 30s), terminate grace (Handlers.pm:607), identity_timeout (Connection.pm:196/211, 5s), resource_timeout and stage_state_age (State.pm:204/630), IPC::wait timeout (IPC.pm:240), preload-map deadline (Runner.pm:1178), plus the Client/Subscriber/logger deadlines. The runner is a long-lived daemon (yath start) where NTP steps and laptop suspend/resume are routine.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Laptop suspends (or NTP steps the clock forward >30s) mid-run and resumes: on the first scheduler tick, _enforce_collector_connect_timeout sees now-since > 30 for every job dispatched just before the suspend and mass-aborts them as 'collector did not connect' even though their collectors connect milliseconds later — the run reports dozens of false FAILures. Connection identity deadlines (5s) simultaneously drop every pending handshake. A backwards step instead freezes those timeouts (a genuinely-hung collector is not failed for step-size extra seconds) and extends the terminate-grace/resource-timeout windows.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Use Time::HiRes::clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) for all interval math in the runner/service/connection layer (keep wall clock only for event stamps), via a small Util shim so the whole codebase switches consistently.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One overstatement: the identity-timeout leg does not "drop every pending handshake" on resume. Connection.pm's expired() is only consulted after the service reads (per the init comment and Role::Service::service_io ordering), so a pre-suspend peer whose identity frame is already readable at resume is identified before expiry can fire; only peers that had not yet written their identity when frozen are dropped. The primary scenario (mass false 'collector did not connect' aborts for jobs in the dispatch->connect window, plus frozen/extended timeouts on backwards steps) is accurate as written.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Downgrade from the audit's P3 to P2: this is user-visible wrong behavior (spurious job failures / dropped handshakes) that is plausible for real users (laptop dev sessions with `yath start` kept running across a lid-close, or systems where NTP steps rather than slews), but it needs an unusual external event (suspend/resume or a large clock step) rather than occurring in a normal single test run or typical short-lived CI job — most CI runners don't suspend and slew-only NTP won't trigger it. No existing TODO_TASKS.md/TODO_STEPS.md entry covers this. Cheap mitigation matches the proposal: swap `Time::HiRes::time()` for `Time::HiRes::clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` in the identified interval-math call sites via a small Util shim (keep wall clock only for event timestamps/log stamps), which is a small, low-risk, centralizable fix.

confirmedFindings.title: A connection closed by a write failure is never removed from the IO::Select set; the poisoned select (EBADF) then starves ALL connections and wedges the runner
confirmedFindings.evidence: Connection::_write and send_control call $self->close on any write failure (eval'd write_frame croak, e.g. EPIPE to a dead peer). close() only closes the fh; it does NOT remove it from the owner's {service_select}. The only paths that call Role::Service::_drop_conn (which does $sel->remove) are (a) the service_io can_read loop, (b) the pending-identity expiry sweep (expired() returns 0 for READY or CLOSED conns), and (c) forward_frame's own failure branch. So a close triggered by service_send (Runner.pm:1127 run_task dispatch, :989/:1068/:1325 stop messages) or by send_control (Handlers.pm _terminate_collector) leaves a closed fh registered in the select set forever. IO::Select caches the fd bits, and select(2) fails with EBADF when any fd in the set is closed. Verified experimentally: with one closed handle in the set, IO::Select->can_read(0) returns 0 handles ($! = 'Bad file descriptor') even though another registered socket has readable data. After that, Role/Service.pm:348 `for my $fh ($sel->can_read(0))` is permanently empty: no connection is ever drained again, no EOF is ever observed, and Connection::expired never fires for established conns.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A preload stage (or a test collector being sent a bail/abort 'terminate' via send_control, or the sampler) crashes; before the runner drains that socket's EOF, the scheduler tick writes to it (service_send 'run_task' / 'stop', or send_control 'terminate') -> EPIPE -> croak caught -> $conn->close, conn left in service_select. Every subsequent can_read(0) fails with EBADF and returns nothing. Collector connections' transitions and EOFs are never read, so no job ever completes its §5.4 EOF decision: `yath test`/`yath run` hangs indefinitely (runner main loop at Runner.pm:1228 keeps ticking but state->done never becomes true), and the persistent runner is permanently deaf to all clients until killed.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Make Connection::close (or the owning service) remove the fh from the select set: e.g. have every close path route through Role::Service::_drop_conn, or add a per-service_io sweep `$self->_drop_conn($conn) for grep { $_->closed } values %{$self->{service_conns}}` before calling can_read. Removing from IO::Select before CORE::close (or sweeping closed conns each tick) fixes both the EBADF poisoning and the stale bookkeeping.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor precision: the wedge is not unconditionally permanent. IO::Select slots are keyed by fd number, so if the freed fd is later reused (e.g. a newly accepted connection at Service.pm:337 replaces the slot, or any reused fd that select reports readable maps back to the stale fh and hits the _drop_conn at Service.pm:353 since drain() on a CLOSED conn returns ()), the poison self-heals. In the cited failure scenario — end of run or all job slots waiting on inbound completion events, so the process allocates no new fds — nothing reuses the fd and the hang is indefinite, so the P1 severity stands. Additional trigger worth noting: inbound conns are set blocking(0) at accept (Service.pm:335), so write_frame croaking with EAGAIN on a full send buffer to a slow-but-alive peer also closes the conn and poisons the select, not just dead-peer EPIPE. The proposal (route close through _drop_conn or sweep closed conns before can_read) is correct.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Upgraded from the audit's recorded P1 to P0: the "wrong result" framing undersells that this isn't isolated to the one dead peer's job — it poisons the shared IO::Select for ALL connections on that service (every other in-flight job's collector, every client socket), so a single ordinary worker death/exit can wedge an entire persistent runner daemon, not just fail one test. Cheap mitigation matches the finding's own proposal and requires no design work: route every close path through Role::Service::_drop_conn (or add `$sel->remove($fh)` directly inside Connection::close, taking $sel as a weak back-reference or via an owner callback), OR have service_io sweep `grep { $_->closed } values %{$self->{service_conns}}` for removal before each can_read(0) call. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this select-poisoning defect specifically (nearby tickets #Tier-7 teardown-dedup item at TODO_TASKS.md:1871 touches close_service/reset_service duplication but not this _write/send_control bypass of _drop_conn) — this needs its own fix, not a byproduct of other planned cleanup.

confirmedFindings.title: PENDING request-id table grows without bound for one-way requests on long-lived connections (persistent runner / sampler memory leak)
confirmedFindings.evidence: send_request unconditionally records `$self->{+PENDING}{$request_id} = 1` for every request; the only deletion is in _classify when a matching response arrives (line 383). The protocol's one-way requests (handler returns undef => no response ever sent: queue_run/queue_task/stop_run/end_queue per Handlers.pm, 'run_task' dispatch Runner.pm:1127, stage->runner outcome reports via StageDelegate.pm:102, and the sampler's periodic 'system_load' pushes, Service/Sampler.pm:231) therefore leave their UUIDs in PENDING forever on connections that live as long as the process.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A persistent (`yath start`) runner: the sampler pushes 'system_load' every tick over one connection for the daemon's lifetime, and the runner sends one 'run_task' per test job per run over each stage connection -- each adds a ~36-byte UUID hash entry that is never removed. Over days/weeks of a persistent runner (or one huge run of 100k+ files on the command's submitter connection) the process memory grows steadily; nothing bounds it.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Only track requests whose caller will wait for a reply: add a `want_reply` flag to send_request (default off for the one-way command set), or cap/expire PENDING entries (they carry a gen_uuid timestamp-free key, so an insertion-order ring or a stamp+sweep works).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor precision: PENDING is per-connection state, so entries are reclaimed when a connection closes. The "one huge run of 100k+ files on the command's submitter connection" variant is therefore self-limiting (the submitter connection closes at run end, freeing its entries); the unbounded-growth scenarios are exactly the daemon-lifetime connections the finding leads with (sampler->runner system_load per tick, runner->stage run_task per dispatched test, stage->runner outcome/job_pid reports). Also note the leak is in the SENDER process of each one-way request (the sampler process, the root runner, each stage host), not the request handler side. Effective per-entry cost is ~100+ bytes (Perl hash entry with 36-char UUID key), not just 36 bytes, so growth is somewhat faster than stated.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap mitigation confirmed feasible and matches the finding's own proposal: add a want_reply=0 default for the five one-way commands (queue_run/queue_task/stop_run/end_queue/run_task) plus Sampler's system_load push, so send_request skips the PENDING insert entirely for fire-and-forget calls -- this is a small, localized change (Connection.pm send_request + the ~6 call sites) with no protocol change since these commands already never get a response. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this specific leak; it is not mentioned among the #64-#105 cleanup-audit items I found, so it would need a new ticket if the team wants to track/fix it. Given it only bites long-lived `yath start` daemons or very large single runs, low urgency (P2) is appropriate but worth a one-line TODO entry since persistent-daemon mode is an intended supported feature of this architecture.

confirmedFindings.title: RunnerReader stamps: record stamps are ignored, and after a harness_process_restart every subsequent event is frozen at the restart's stamp
confirmedFindings.evidence: _wrap uses `stamp => $self->{+LAST_STAMP} // time`. LAST_STAMP is set ONLY by harness_process_restart (line 112) and harness_process_exit (line 127); ordinary records never update it and their own stamps (e.g. $fd->{trace}{stamp}, which the sibling JobReader::_stamp_for explicitly harvests, JobReader.pm:102-108) are ignored. So before any restart, events are stamped with the tailer's read time rather than the record's time (wrong for replay/log import of an existing file); and once a resumable stage collector writes a harness_process_restart (which the POD says does NOT end the stream), LAST_STAMP is defined forever after, so every later stage-output event carries the restart's wall-clock stamp.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Persistent runner with a reloading/restarting preload stage: the stage restarts at 10:00; the stage keeps producing output for hours; every stage-events record rendered/logged after that (including into the DB via log import) is stamped 10:00. Renderers, duration math, and DB ordering on stamp show hours of output collapsed onto the restart instant.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Mirror JobReader: derive the stamp per record (trace/harness facet stamps first, falling back to `time`), i.e. only use LAST_STAMP as a fallback that is also refreshed by each record's own stamp -- not as a sticky override.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: The core bug is the sticky post-restart stamp; the secondary claim (pre-restart events stamped with tailer read time being wrong for replay/log import) is currently moot since Renderer::Base is RunnerReader's only caller and `yath stop` tail mode skips pre-existing records — no log-import path instantiates RunnerReader today. Fix as proposed: mirror JobReader::_stamp_for (harvest the record's own facet/trace stamp, refreshing LAST_STAMP, with LAST_STAMP//time only as fallback).

confirmedFindings.title: Runner::Subscriber connect/subscribe has no runner-liveness escape: a runner that dies after binding the socket costs the command a fixed 30s stall
confirmedFindings.evidence: Runner::Client::connection breaks out of its connect-retry loop via the caller-supplied liveness_check (Runner/Client.pm:222-225) precisely so a dead runner does not cost the full CONNECT_TIMEOUT. Subscriber::_connect has the identical retry loop (Subscriber.pm:207-214) but NO liveness check, and subscribe's reply-wait loop (lines 141-163) likewise only times out after CONNECT_TIMEOUT=30s -- the stale runner.socket file left by the dead runner keeps `-S $path` true while connect_unix gets ECONNREFUSED, so every retry fails for the full 30 seconds. App::Yath2::Client::connect_subscriber (which has access to runner_gone) just evals subscribe and warns.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath test` with a preload that crashes the runner right after runner.socket is bound (the exact case Command/test.pm's own comment names): submit_queue succeeds (one-way frames), then connect_subscriber spins connect-ECONNREFUSED against the stale socket for a flat 30 seconds before warning and falling back to the no-subscriber path. User sees yath sit silent for 30s after a fast runner crash instead of reporting the failure within a poll interval.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Give Subscriber the same optional liveness_check attribute Runner::Client has (App::Yath2::Client already owns runner_gone and can pass it in connect_subscriber), checked each retry iteration in _connect and in the subscribe reply-wait loop.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One cited locus is overstated: the subscribe reply-wait loop (Subscriber.pm:141-164) does NOT cost 30s for a dead runner — runner death after accepting the connection produces EOF, $conn->closed goes true, and the croak at line 159 fires within one drain cycle; a liveness check there only helps against a hung-but-alive runner. The entire 30s stall lives in _connect (lines 207-215) against the stale socket. An equally valid fix is Client::connect_subscriber short-circuiting on $self->runner_gone before/while subscribing, since runner_gone reaps the zombie first so kill(0) is accurate.

confirmedFindings.title: Util::Queue is dead code in 2.0d: Runner.pm/run.pm/stop.pm only `use` it, never instantiate it — the live queue seam is socket-based
confirmedFindings.evidence: grep -rn 'Queue->new' across lib/ (excluding reference/ and worktrees) matches only the POD synopsis inside Queue.pm itself. Runner.pm:14, run.pm:10, stop.pm:12 contain bare `use Test2::Harness2::Util::Queue` with no method calls. stop.pm:65 `$self->client->submitter->end_queue` resolves to Runner/Client.pm:140 `_send('end_queue')` (unix-socket request), handled by Runner/State.pm:277 setting a QUEUE_ENDED flag — no queue.jsonl file involved. Runner.pm:452 comment confirms 'The transient path does not write queue.jsonl/jobs.jsonl'. t/unit/App/Yath2/RunPlan.t:7 likewise only loads it.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: No runtime failure today — but the module ships on CPAN with POD advertising a multi-process contract, and every finding below is armed in it. Anyone (including a future chunk of the 2.0d evolve plan) who follows the module's own SYNOPSIS re-enters all the races below. The three stale `use` lines also mislead auditors and readers into believing these commands consume the file queue.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Either delete lib/Test2/Harness2/Util/Queue.pm (and the three stale imports plus RunPlan.t:7) or fix the latent bugs below before any code revives it. At minimum remove the leftover `use` statements from Runner.pm, run.pm, stop.pm.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One scope note: Queue IS still actively used (instantiated in Collector.pm/State.pm) in the stale worktrees under worktrees/collectors-everywhere and .claude/worktrees/*, so deletion should be done on 2.0d only and those worktrees left alone (or pruned separately). Also run.pm:10 uses the non-empty import form (`use ...;` without `()`), a trivial cosmetic difference from the other two; all three are equally dead.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Already tracked: TODO_TASKS.md line ~1882-1892 has a proposed cleanup task (effort S, risk low) that explicitly cites this exact finding's evidence ('Queue confirmed dead by finding evidence') and prescribes deleting Queue.pm plus the four bare `use` lines (Runner.pm:14, run.pm:10, stop.pm:12, and t/unit/App/Yath2/RunPlan.t:7 — the finding missed this fourth site, already covered by the existing ticket). No new ticket needed; just execute #1882 when doing cleanup passes. Not refuted because the trigger (misleading imports / latent-reactivation risk) is real and present in the code, just correctly rated as lowest-severity latent/cosmetic issue.

confirmedFindings.title: Stream::write seek arguments are transposed: seek($fh,2,0) seeks to absolute offset 2 (SEEK_SET) instead of end-of-file (SEEK_END)
confirmedFindings.evidence: Stream.pm:80 `seek($fh,2,0);` — Perl's seek(FH, POSITION, WHENCE) with Fcntl SEEK_SET=0/SEEK_END=2, so this positions the handle at byte 2 from the start; the intent (seek to end before appending) requires seek($fh,0,2). It is masked today only because both open paths (Stream.pm:73 lock_file '>>' and :76 open_file '>>') use O_APPEND, which forces every write(2) to the end regardless of the file position.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Latent until the open mode changes or the file lives on a filesystem where the append guarantee is weak (O_APPEND on NFS is emulated client-side): writer process W2 appending to a queue/log written by W1 would then position at offset 2 and overwrite W1's bytes 2..N — a reader process polling the file sees its already-consumed region rewritten and decode-confesses, or silently reads clobbered tasks. Also misleads every future maintainer reading the write path.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Change to `seek($fh, 0, SEEK_END);` (Fcntl is already imported in this file) or delete the line entirely with a comment that '>>' guarantees appends.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two corrections: (1) the NFS leg of the failure scenario is wrong — NFS clients emulate O_APPEND by writing at the (stale) server EOF, not at the fd's seek position, so writes would never land at offset 2 even there; the only reachable failure requires a future edit changing the open mode away from '>>'. The real value is deleting/fixing an incorrect, misleading line before that happens. (2) The proposal's "Fcntl is already imported" is imprecise: line 9 imports only SEEK_SET, so SEEK_END must be added to the import list — or simply delete line 80 with a comment that '>>' guarantees appends (preferred, matches the legacy-inherited nature of the line).
confirmedFindings.severity_note: This exact defect is already tracked: TODO_TASKS.md:1884-1889 (audit item covering Util/File/Stream.pm) independently identifies "a transposed seek($fh,2,0) at line 80 (absolute byte 2, not EOF — masked by '>>' mode)" and the planned fix is to delete the line entirely as part of a broader Stream.pm cleanup (removing the dead -tail attribute, dead public seek(), and the dead use_write_lock branch), with the explicit note "append mode already positions at EOF; if kept use seek($fh,0,SEEK_END)". No separate fix needed — it will be resolved in passing when that TODO item is executed. No new ticket required.

confirmedFindings.title: yath spawn command exits 0 (false success) when the supervisor dies without sending exit_status
confirmedFindings.evidence: bridge_io initializes `my $status = 0;` then loops `my $msg = $ctl->read_message; last if $ctl->closed && !$msg;` (spawn.pm:291-300). A control-channel EOF without an exit_status frame falls out of the loop with status still 0, so parse_exit(0) reports a clean exit and run() calls exit(0) (spawn.pm:261). The Control.pm POD itself states 'the command never sees an EOF before the exit_status frame on a healthy run', i.e. EOF-without-status is by definition an unhealthy run, yet it is mapped to success. Supervisor-side paths that close the channel without a status: fork failure `my $child = fork() // do { warn ...; POSIX::_exit(1) }` (JobLauncher.pm:143) exits after the fd handshake with no exit_status; the command-death branch `POSIX::_exit(0)` at JobLauncher.pm:181; and any SIGKILL/OOM/crash of the detached supervisor.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Stage machine hits the process limit (EAGAIN from fork) when launching the spawn supervisor's script child: the supervisor has already completed the fd pass, so the command is past _accept_supervisor; the supervisor _exit(1)s, the control socket EOFs, and `yath spawn myapp.pl` prints nothing and exits 0 — the user's script never ran but the command reports success. Same false-0 if the supervisor is OOM-killed mid-run: the script child keeps running detached on the user's terminal while the command returns exit 0 and the shell prompt comes back under it.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In bridge_io, treat `$ctl->closed` without a received exit_status frame as a failure: die/print 'spawn supervisor vanished before reporting an exit status' and exit non-zero (e.g. 255), reserving exit 0 for an actual exit_status of 0.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: yath spawn exits 0 (false success) when the spawn supervisor dies between sending the hello frame and sending exit_status. bridge_io (lib/App/Yath2/Command/spawn.pm:291-300) treats control-channel EOF-without-exit_status as status 0; run() then exit(0)s (spawn.pm:261). Valid triggers: supervisor SIGKILL/OOM/crash mid-run (the setsid'd script child keeps running detached while the shell prompt returns under exit 0), or Control::_send failure in send_exit_status (JobLauncher.pm:192), which closes the channel without a frame. NOT triggered by JobLauncher.pm:143 fork failure (exits before send_hello, caught by the hello guard at spawn.pm:285-287) nor by JobLauncher.pm:181 (command already dead). Fix as proposed: track whether an exit_status frame was actually received in bridge_io and die/exit non-zero (e.g. 255) with a 'spawn supervisor vanished before reporting an exit status' message when the channel closes without one.

confirmedFindings.title: recv_fds busy-spins forever at 100% CPU on peer EOF when errno is EINTR (IO::FDPass::recv leaves errno untouched on EOF)
confirmedFindings.evidence: recv_fds's retry loop is `while (1) { $fd = IO::FDPass::recv($sockfd); last if defined $fd && $fd >= 0; next if $! == EINTR; last; }` (FdPass.pm:189-194). Empirically verified against installed IO::FDPass 1.3: on peer EOF recvmsg returns 0 and IO::FDPass::recv returns -1 WITHOUT modifying errno. So if errno is EINTR when EOF is hit, `next if $! == EINTR` retries, recv instantly returns -1 again with the same stale errno, and the loop never exits. Reproduced end-to-end in a test: a Perl-level signal handler interrupts the blocking recv (Perl installs handlers without SA_RESTART, hence the EINTR retry existing at all), the peer closes before the retry, and the loop spun for the full watchdog window ('SPIN CONFIRMED'). recv_fds also never resets $! before the first call, so any pre-existing EINTR in errno triggers the same spin if the peer is already gone.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: yath spawn: command is killed (Ctrl-C — its signal forwarding is not installed until after hello, spawn.pm:289) while the detached supervisor is blocked in recv_fds($sock,3) at JobLauncher.pm:129 and any Perl-handled signal (e.g. the inherited stage-host HUP handler during a `yath reload`) interrupts the recv first: the supervisor spins forever at 100% CPU as a detached setsid process that nothing ever reaps or kills, never forking the script and never exiting. Interactive mode has the same shape at Interactive.pm:114 in the test child when the accept-loop parent exits mid-handshake — the test child pegs a core until the silence timeout (if enabled) kills it.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In the retry loops of recv_fds (and symmetrically send_fds), set `$! = 0` immediately before each IO::FDPass call so a -1 return with unchanged errno (the EOF case) is never mistaken for EINTR; the existing croak with 'sender closed before sending all fds' then fires correctly.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One scenario detail is imprecise: after POSIX::setsid() the supervisor is in its own session and process group, so a `yath reload` HUP to the runner/stage tree or a terminal-generated signal does not automatically reach it; the inherited HUP handler only matters if a signal is addressed to the supervisor's pid directly. The more robust trigger needing no signal delivery at all is the one also cited in the evidence: recv_fds never clears $! before the FIRST IO::FDPass::recv call, and errno carries across fork from the stage host (whose IPC signal handlers make interrupted-syscall EINTR a common resting errno value), so a command that dies between accept and send_fds spins the supervisor immediately. Interactive.pm:114 has the same defect but a milder blast radius (test child, possibly bounded by silence timeout). Fix as proposed: set $! = 0 immediately before each IO::FDPass::recv/send call in both loops.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap, essentially free mitigation: in recv_fds's (and send_fds's) retry loop, set `local $! = 0;` (or `$! = 0;`) immediately before each IO::FDPass call, so a -1 return with unchanged errno can never be mistaken for EINTR — the existing croak('sender closed before sending all fds') then fires as intended. No existing TODO_TASKS.md item names this specific FdPass EINTR/EOF interaction; the nearby #81 entry (FdPass/IPC/Connection dead-code & duplication cleanup) and the generic "_drain_transitions spin" quick-fix are related-in-spirit but do not cover this bug, so it is not already slated for a fix in passing. Worth also checking, as a follow-up beyond this review, whether JobLauncher's launch_spawn should `delete @SIG{qw/INT HUP TERM CHLD/}` after setsid (as IPC.pm:stop() does) so the detached supervisor doesn't run inherited handlers that close over a stale parent IPC object at all — that would remove the EINTR-generating precondition at its source rather than only patching the errno race.

confirmedFindings.title: Interactive-mode wrapper exits 0 when the yath command child dies by signal ($? >> 8 discards the signal)
confirmedFindings.evidence: The fd-pass accept-loop parent (the process the user's shell actually waits on in interactive mode) reaps the real yath command child with `my $got = waitpid($pid, POSIX::WNOHANG()); $finish->($? >> 8) if $got == $pid;` (Debug.pm:372-373). For a signal death $? is the signal number in the low 7 bits and the high byte is 0, so `$? >> 8` is 0 and $finish exits 0. Contrast App::Yath2::Command::spawn::run (spawn.pm:253-261), which parses the raw status and re-raises the signal.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath test -i ...` — the forked yath command child is OOM-SIGKILLed (or segfaults) mid-run: the interactive wrapper parent reaps it, computes 9 >> 8 == 0, unlinks the socket and exits 0. The shell/CI sees a successful yath invocation even though the run was killed with tests unexecuted.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Use parse_exit on the raw $? in _interactive_accept_loop: exit non-zero (e.g. 128+sig) or re-raise the signal when the child died by signal, mirroring spawn.pm's handling.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Scenario and lines are accurate as written. Minor precision: the vulnerable expression is on line 373 (`$finish->($? >> 8) if $got == $pid;`), with waitpid on 372. Fix as proposed: parse the raw $? (Test2::Harness2::Util::parse_exit, already used by spawn.pm) and exit 128+sig or re-raise the signal when the child died by signal.

confirmedFindings.title: Spawn supervisor's command-death path sends one TERM then blocks in waitpid forever (no KILL escalation, and pgroup-kill races the child's setsid)
confirmedFindings.evidence: On control EOF the supervisor does `kill('-TERM', $child); local $?; waitpid($child, 0); POSIX::_exit(0);` (JobLauncher.pm:175-181): a single TERM to the process group, then an unbounded blocking waitpid with no TERM->KILL escalation — unlike every other teardown in the codebase (e.g. Preload::Host::stop, Host.pm:444-455, which TERMs, waits 5s, then KILLs). Two ways the TERM never takes effect: (1) the script child only becomes its own pgroup at POSIX::setsid() (JobLauncher.pm:153), which runs after the fork at :143 — if the command died before hello (its signal forwarding is only installed after the hello exchange, spawn.pm:289, so a plain Ctrl-C kills it), the supervisor can reach the EOF branch on its first poll before the child has setsid'd; `kill('-TERM', $child)` then targets a nonexistent pgroup, returns 0 unchecked, and nothing is signaled; (2) the spawned script traps or ignores SIGTERM.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath spawn server.pl` (a daemon that traps TERM for graceful shutdown but wedges, or simply a script racing its setsid) and hits Ctrl-C during launch: the command dies, the supervisor's EOF branch fires, the TERM is lost or ignored, and waitpid blocks forever — the ARCHITECTURE §4.8 contract 'command death kills the spawned process group' is broken: the script runs on indefinitely attached to the freed terminal, and the detached supervisor is a permanent stuck process that survives harness teardown.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In the EOF branch: check kill's return / retry against the child pid as well as the pgroup, and replace the blocking waitpid with a bounded wait (e.g. WNOHANG poll for ~5s) followed by KILL escalation, matching the stop() pattern used elsewhere. Optionally have the supervisor setpgid the child itself right after fork to close the setsid race.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor corrections only: the escalation-pattern comparison file is lib/Test2/Harness2/Preload/Host.pm (stop(), lines 444-455), not Runner/Preload/Host.pm. Scope note: because the supervisor is already detached from the harness by design, the failure leaks one permanently-stuck supervisor process plus a runaway script attached to the freed terminal per occurrence, but does not block harness teardown or any harness-side loop — P3 is the right severity. The proposed fix (bounded WNOHANG wait with TERM→KILL escalation, checking kill's return and signaling the child pid as well as the pgroup, or having the supervisor setpgid the child immediately after fork to close the setsid race) is sound; setpgid-after-fork in both parent and child is the standard fix for the race half.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Split the finding: drop or heavily discount the setsid-race half (1) — practically unreachable given the relative timing (single setsid() syscall in the child vs. full remote-process-death + socket-EOF-detection latency needed to enter the EOF branch); keep it only as a hardening note (e.g. have the supervisor setpgid the child right after fork to remove the race entirely, per the finding's own proposal). The real, actionable defect is half (2): no bounded-wait + KILL escalation on the EOF/command-death path. Cheap mitigation: mirror the existing Preload::Host::stop pattern already in this codebase — send TERM, WNOHANG-poll waitpid for ~5s, then send KILL and do a final blocking waitpid — instead of `kill('-TERM',$child); waitpid($child,0)`. No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry covers this specific gap (checked; TIER 5 spawn/#39 section covers spawn design but not TERM/KILL escalation in the supervisor's death path), so this is a fresh, valid finding worth fixing in passing.

confirmedFindings.title: Interactive listen socket passes the real terminal STDIN fd to any connector with no peer identity check, and the path is broadcast in every test's environment
confirmedFindings.evidence: The accept loop passes STDIN to the first (and every) connection unconditionally: `my $conn = $listen->accept or next; _interactive_pass_stdin($conn);` (Debug.pm:378-379) with no handshake or identity frame — contrast the Role::Service transport, which requires an identity preamble. The socket path is advertised in the run env and the command's own %ENV (`$settings->run->env_vars->{YATH_INTERACTIVE} = $path; $ENV{YATH_INTERACTIVE} = $path;`, Debug.pm:338-341), so every test AND every descendant process a test forks inherits it for the lifetime of the whole run; Interactive::connect_stdin (Interactive.pm:104-128) will dial and take the fd from any such process.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: During `yath test -i`, test A forks a background helper/daemon that inherits YATH_INTERACTIVE and later (directly or via a re-exec of a perl that does -MTest2::Harness2::Interactive, or any code calling connect_stdin) dials the socket while test B is the interactive test: the accept loop hands the daemon a duplicate of the user's real terminal STDIN descriptor. Both processes now read the same terminal — the user's keystrokes intended for test B's prompt are nondeterministically consumed by the stale daemon, wedging the interactive session with no diagnostic.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Add a minimal identity/nonce check before send_fds: put a per-run secret in the env alongside the path (or require the dialer to write a one-line token that the accept loop verifies against the currently-dispatched job) and only pass the fd on a match; log and drop non-matching connections.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: The scenario's trigger is narrower than stated: merely inheriting YATH_INTERACTIVE does not cause a dial. The stray descendant must actually invoke connect_stdin — i.e., load Test2::Harness2::Interactive (whose import auto-connects when the env var is set), be a nested harness-launched perl (-MTest2::Harness2::Interactive is only injected by yath's own JobLauncher), or otherwise call connect_stdin explicitly. So the realistic vector is harness-aware descendants (e.g., a test that runs a nested yath, or forked code that loads the Interactive module), not arbitrary daemons. Everything else in the finding is accurate: no peer check before send_fds, path broadcast run-wide, env var never cleared post-connect, and a rogue connect silently splits terminal input with the genuine interactive test. P3 with the narrowed trigger.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap mitigation matches the proposal: since interactive is -j1 and the accept loop already knows which single job is currently dispatched, tag the job's env_vars with a per-job nonce and have the accept loop require the dialer to echo it before send_fds, dropping/logging non-matching connections -- small, localized change. No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry found specific to this socket; interactive mode's docs already disclaim it as best-effort/manual-only (no controlling terminal, breaks plugins needing STDIN), consistent with treating this as a narrow edge case rather than a mainstream hardening gap.

confirmedFindings.title: Replay of a truncated compressed log crashes with internal 'cannot seek backwards' error instead of the incomplete-log diagnostic
confirmedFindings.evidence: Util/File.pm read_line does `seek($fh,$pos,SEEK_SET) or die ... if eof($fh) || tell($fh) != $pos` (line 92-93). For a .jsonl.gz/.jsonl.bz2 log the fh is an IO::Uncompress handle (Util.pm open_file lines 302-327) which only supports forward seeks. Empirically confirmed with a probe script driving JSONLFileProducer over a gzip log whose compressed stream was cut short (simulating a killed writer): the producer poll dies with 'IO::Uncompress::Gunzip::seek: cannot seek backwards at .../Test2/Harness2/Util/File.pm line 92.' after rendering the decodable prefix. A truncated PLAIN .jsonl log by contrast finishes cleanly and replay dies with the intended "Log did not contain final data!" message (replay.pm:84-85). The crash propagates out of $loop->start (replay.pm:78), so $loop->finish / renderer finish never run.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath test --gzip ...` is killed mid-run (SIGKILL/crash), leaving log.jsonl.gz with a truncated gzip stream (IO::Compress::Gzip never flushed/terminated). User runs `yath replay log.jsonl.gz`: some events render, then the command aborts with the cryptic internal error 'IO::Uncompress::Gunzip::seek: cannot seek backwards at .../Util/File.pm line 92' (exit 255), renderers are never finalized, and the user gets no indication the actual problem is an incomplete log — unlike the plain-.jsonl case which reports 'Log did not contain final data!'.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In Util::File::read_line, skip the eof/tell seek re-sync for non-seekable (IO::Uncompress) handles, or wrap the compressed-stream EOF/error in an eval that marks the stream done; JSONLFileProducer should treat a decompression-stream error as EOF so replay reaches its existing 'Log did not contain final data!' diagnostic.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Precise mechanism: truncation leaves a trailing partial decoded line; read_line's hold-off (File.pm line 101) returns without advancing LINE_POS while the handle's tell has advanced past the partial line, so the NEXT read_line sees tell($fh) != $pos and attempts a backward seek, which the tied IO::Uncompress handle croaks on (it is the tell-mismatch arm of line 93, not the eof arm). Boundary note: if truncation happens to land exactly on a decompressed newline boundary (no partial line), the compressed case also finishes cleanly and reaches the intended diagnostic; the crash requires a partial trailing line, which is the common case for arbitrary truncation. The proposed fix direction (treat non-seekable stream mismatch/error as EOF so replay reaches the existing diagnostic) is sound.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket covers this. Cheap mitigation matching the finding's own proposal: in Util::File::read_line, detect a non-seekable/IO::Uncompress handle (or wrap the seek call in eval) and on failure treat the stream as done/EOF rather than dying, so JSONLFileProducer/replay falls through to the existing 'Log did not contain final data!' diagnostic — this is a small, localized fix (a capability check or eval around the seek at File.pm:92-93) with no architectural risk, worth folding in alongside any nearby Util/File.pm or replay.pm cleanup work.

confirmedFindings.title: yath reload is fire-and-forget: prints success and exits 0 with no acknowledgment that anything reloaded, including on a no-preload runner where HUP is an explicit no-op
confirmedFindings.evidence: reload.pm run() (lines 27-44) deletes the BLACKLIST file, prints "Sending SIGHUP to $pid", kill('HUP', $pid), and returns 0. There is no socket request, no wait, and no readback of any kind — success is reported the instant the signal is queued. On the receive side, Runner.pm's HUP handler (lines 190-212) is an explicit `return;` no-op when there is no preload root (comment at 209-211: 'a no-preload persistent runner must be restarted to pick up code changes'), and even the preload path only enqueues a 'reload_root' service_send with no reply consumed by the command. (This is the COMMAND-side gap, distinct from the already-filed _preload_root_stage_identity pid bug.)
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath start` with no --preload, later runs `yath reload`: output is 'Deleting module blacklist...' (if present) and 'Sending SIGHUP to <pid>', exit 0 — but the runner's HUP handler does nothing at all and no stage exists to reload. The user believes the runner picked up code changes; the stale runner keeps serving. Same silent-success occurs whenever the runner-side reload fails for any reason, since the command never observes an acknowledgment.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Route reload through the runner socket as a request/response (the Client/service channel already exists) so the command can report which stages reloaded, and have the command print an explicit 'this runner has no preload stages; restart it to pick up changes' warning (nonzero exit or at least a warning) when the runner reports nothing to reload.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two sharpening points: (1) the silent-failure surface is wider than stated — even with preloads, the HUP handler silently returns if _preload_root_stage_identity fails, and service_send has no reply, so the command reports success in every failure mode, not just no-preload; (2) the command's POD/description ("forcing it to reload") directly contradicts the no-preload no-op, so a doc fix is needed alongside the proposed socket round-trip. Severity is UX-only (no crash/data loss, recoverable by restart) — P3, borderline P2 given the stale-runner-serving-old-code footgun after apparent success.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Bump from the finding's own P2 guess to P1: the no-preload persistent-runner configuration is explicitly supported and simple (no --preload setup needed), so 'reload a no-preload runner' is an everyday sequence, not an edge case — and the always-silent success (no ack) applies universally, including when a preload-side reload fails. No existing TODO_TASKS.md/TODO_STEPS.md ticket covers this specific command-side ack gap; the nearby chunk-10/19 entries in TODO_STEPS.md describe the reload *routing* implementation (base-stage channel translating HUP into in-run respawn) but not the client-side acknowledgment/exit-code problem. Cheap mitigation: reload.pm could check pfile metadata (already used elsewhere to distinguish no-preload vs preload runners) and print an explicit 'this runner has no preload stages; restart it to pick up code changes' warning without needing the full request/response socket plumbing — that alone would close most of the practical harm cheaply, with the full ack/round-trip fix being the more thorough follow-up.

confirmedFindings.title: Replay job filter that matches nothing is silently ignored: zero events stream, but the full-run final table and exit code render as if no filter was given
confirmedFindings.evidence: replay.pm:61 builds the filter as an exact-match hash of raw argv strings; JSONLFileProducer poll drops every non-matching event (line 141) but always captures harness_final (line 136-139), and _match_job (173-189) only maps exact rel_file/abs_file/file strings. Nothing ever checks whether any filter key matched a job. replay.pm:87-90 then renders render_final_data($final_data) — the recorded WHOLE-run rollup, including failures for jobs the user filtered out — and exits on the whole run's pass/fail. Job ids in logs are uppercase UUIDs (gen_uuid) so a lowercase paste also never matches.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath replay log.jsonl t/passing.t` where the user's path spelling differs from the recorded rel_file (e.g. './t/passing.t' vs 't/passing.t', a lowercase job uuid, or a typo): zero job events are rendered with no 'no jobs matched' warning, yet the final table still lists every failed job in the run and the command exits 1 (the whole run failed) — the user cannot tell whether their selected job passed, or that their filter never matched anything.
confirmedFindings.proposal: After the loop, warn (or die) for each filter arg that never matched a job id or file (the producer already mutates $jobs when a file matches, so unmatched keys are detectable); consider filtering the rendered final_data/exit to the selected jobs or documenting that the summary is whole-run.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Narrow the defect: the whole-run final table and whole-run exit code are intended and documented behavior (producer POD: "the recorded harness_final always passes through", "matching the original replay behavior"), and the code is a faithful port of legacy 1.0 (reference/pre_ai_2.0/lib/App/Yath/Command/replay.pm:88-107, identical logic). The actionable bug is only the missing "no jobs matched" / per-arg unmatched-filter diagnostic, inherited from 1.0. Note also that the producer is documented as a transition shim to be replaced by the DB-backed archive producer, so the fix belongs in replay.pm (post-loop check of which $jobs keys were never promoted/matched) rather than in the producer.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap mitigation matches the finding's own proposal: after the poll loop finishes (producer done), warn for any filter key in $jobs that was never satisfied — the producer already mutates $jobs->{$job_id}=1 on a file match in _match_job, so any original key still absent (or absent from the set of ever-seen job_ids) is a detectable "this filter argument matched nothing" condition; emit a warning distinguishable from a legitimately-empty replay. No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry covers this specific issue — #89 (test.pm/replay render sharing) and #92-area entries nearby are about code-duplication/dead-code cleanup in replay.pm/JSONLFileProducer.pm, not this filter-vs-final-data correctness gap, so this would need its own follow-up item. Worth separately noting even matching filters still render the unfiltered whole-run final_data table/exit code (not scoped to selected jobs), which contradicts the command's own docs ("only listed jobs will be processed") — a second, related P2-level UX issue the same fix pass should consider.

confirmedFindings.title: A single corrupt line aborts the entire replay with a confess from deep in Util::File; skip_bad_decode exists but the replay producer never enables it
confirmedFindings.evidence: Util/File.pm read_line confesses on any line that fails JSON decode unless SKIP_BAD_DECODE is set (line 110), and JSONLFileProducer->stream (line 170) constructs the JSONL reader without skip_bad_decode. Empirically confirmed: a log with one non-JSON line between valid events makes producer->poll die with 'JSON decode error: malformed JSON string ... at .../Util/JSON.pm line 71' (confess with stack trace); zero further events render and $loop->finish never runs.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: A 50k-event log has one garbled line (partial write from the crashed writer that later got more data appended, disk corruption, or an editor touch). `yath replay big.jsonl` renders events up to that line then aborts with a JSON-decode stack trace (exit 255); everything after the bad line — including the recorded harness_final and failure table — is unreachable, and there is no flag to skip the bad line.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Construct the replay stream with skip_bad_decode => 2 (warn and continue) or add a --strict/--lenient replay option; at minimum catch the decode error in poll and die with a one-line 'log line N is corrupt' message instead of a confess.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Minor scenario correction: poll reads batches of up to 1000 lines, and the die occurs before the batch is returned, so valid events in the same batch preceding the bad line are also lost — only prior fully-returned batches render, not strictly "events up to that line". Cited files/lines are otherwise accurate; proposal (skip_bad_decode => 2 on the replay stream, or a lenient flag / one-line error) is sound.

confirmedFindings.title: yath reload with a live socket but missing/garbled workdir PID file crashes with "Can't kill a non-numeric process ID" after printing 'Sending SIGHUP to <blank>'
confirmedFindings.evidence: Discovery::pid returns undef when $workdir/PID is missing or does not hold digits (Discovery.pm:250-258 — the PID file is written by the runner 'as it boots', separate from the socket bind, and can be missing in the start race or after tmp-reaper cleanup). Pfile->find only validates the SOCKET is live, never that pid is defined. reload.pm:41 interpolates the undef pid into 'Sending SIGHUP to ' (uninitialized-value warning) and line 42 calls kill('HUP', $data->{pid}) — verified: perl croaks "Can't kill a non-numeric process ID" on an undef pid, so the command dies with that message, which names neither the PID file nor the workdir.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Runner workdir PID file was removed by a tmpwatch/systemd-tmpfiles cleanup (or reload races a just-started runner before the PID write): `yath reload` prints 'Deleting module blacklist...', then 'Sending SIGHUP to ' with a blank pid plus an uninitialized warning, then dies 'Can't kill a non-numeric process ID at .../reload.pm line 42' — exit 255 with no hint that the workdir PID file is the problem or that the runner is otherwise healthy.
confirmedFindings.proposal: In reload.pm, `my $pid = $pfile->pid; die "Runner found at <workdir> but its PID file is missing/unreadable; restart the runner.\n" unless $pid;` before printing/killing (same guard belongs in stop/kill paths that use Discovery pid as a signal fallback).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Drop the start-race trigger: Runner::process writes the PID file atomically (Runner.pm:438-439, write_file_atomic of "$$") BEFORE start_service binds runner.socket (line 454), and the pid survives the reload exec — so a socket that accepts a connect guarantees the PID file was already written. The only reachable triggers are external: tmp-reaper/manual deletion of the workdir PID file while the socket stays live, permission loss, or corrupted (empty/non-digit) content. Extend the fix beyond reload: stop.pm has the same croak on undef pid at line 58 (client->attach_runner($pid)) and line 72 (sleep 0.02 while kill(0, $pid)), sourced from pfile_data->{pid} at stop.pm:46 with no defined-check.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Lower confidence than the finding implies: the 'start race' and 'tmp-reaper cleanup' scenarios in the evidence aren't actually supported by the code — PID is written atomically before the socket binds (Runner.pm ~line 438, before start_service), and a dead runner's stale symlink is cleaned/skipped by Discovery->find rather than left presenting a resolving socket. So this only fires under external interference with the workdir (bad tmpwatch/tmpfiles rule matching just the PID file, disk-full during the atomic rename, manual deletion), which is why P3 (latent/theoretical) rather than P1/P2. Cheap mitigation still worth taking in passing since it's a 2-line guard: in reload.pm, `my $pid = $data->{pid} // die "Runner found at $data->{dir} but its PID file is missing/unreadable; restart the runner.\n";` before the print/kill, so the failure names the workdir instead of surfacing Perl's internal kill() croak. Same Discovery::pid consumers in stop/kill paths (if any use it as a signal fallback) would benefit from the identical guard. No existing TODO_TASKS.md entry found for this specific gap.

confirmedFindings.title: Symlinked test directories are silently skipped by the finder's File::Find scan; their tests never run and the run still exits 0
confirmedFindings.evidence: Finder.pm:657 calls File::Find::find({no_chdir => 1, wanted => ...}, @dirs) with no `follow`/`follow_fast`, so File::Find neither descends into symlinked subdirectories nor into a symlink passed as a top-level search dir. Empirically verified on this host (perl probe in scratchpad): a dir containing `t/linked -> ../../real/t` yields only the non-symlinked file, and a top-level symlink-to-dir search arg yields zero files (only the symlink node itself is visited, no descent). Meanwhile Finder.pm:615 (`push @dirs => $path and next if -d $path;`) happily accepts a symlinked dir as a search dir because -d follows the link, so the user gets no 'not a valid file or directory' error either. Nothing downstream (RunPlan::populate, Client::submit_queue) can notice files that were never produced. If the symlink was the ONLY search path, populate returns 0 and test.pm:202 `return unless $pop;` bails with exit 1 but prints no explanation at all.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: Repo layout: `t/unit/*.t` plus `t/integration -> ../shared/integration-tests` (a symlinked subdir holding 40 .t files). `yath test t/` discovers and runs only t/unit; every integration test is silently absent from the plan, no warning or skip record is emitted, and the run exits 0 because all discovered tests pass. Variant: `yath test t xt` where `xt` is a symlink to a shared author-test dir runs zero xt tests with exit 0. Degenerate variant: `yath test xt` (symlink as the only path) exits 1 with no output explaining that 0 tests were found.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Pass `follow => 1` (or `follow_fast => 1` with `follow_skip => 2`) to File::Find::find, or pre-resolve symlinked dirs; at minimum resolve top-level @dirs entries via realpath before handing them to File::Find, and print a 'no tests found in <dir>' diagnostic when a search dir contributes zero files (and a message before the `return unless $pop` in Command/test.pm).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Downgrade P1 -> P2 and note this is not a 2.0d regression: the identical File::Find call (no follow, no_chdir=1) exists in the legacy reference finder (reference/pre_ai_2.0/lib/App/Yath/Finder.pm:666-683), so yath 1.x has always behaved this way, and not descending into symlinked dirs is also the conventional default of File::Find/GNU find. The truly silent exit-0 case requires the symlinked dir to be a subdir of a scanned dir alongside other passing tests; when the symlink is the only/explicit search path the run does exit nonzero (1), just with no explanatory output. Symlinked files listed inside scanned dirs ARE found (File::Find visits symlink-to-file entries and -f follows them), narrowing the bug strictly to directory symlinks. Fix note: plain follow => 1 dies on symlink loops/duplicates unless follow_skip => 2 is also set; pre-resolving @dirs via realpath at Finder.pm:615 plus a zero-tests diagnostic before test.pm:202 is the safer minimal remedy.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Cheap mitigation matches the proposal: add `follow_fast => 1, follow_skip => 2` (safer than plain `follow => 1`, which dies on symlink loops without follow_skip) to the File::Find::find call at Finder.pm:657, and/or realpath-resolve top-level @dirs entries before the -d check at line 615. Additionally cheap: emit a 'no tests found under <dir>' warning per zero-yield search dir, and print a diagnostic before `return unless $pop` in test.pm:202 so the degenerate silent-exit-1 case isn't silent. No existing TODO_TASKS.md/TODO_STEPS.md entry covers this — grepped both files for symlink/File::Find/follow, only unrelated runner-socket-symlink-discovery hits found, so this would need a new task if adopted.

confirmedFindings.title: --exclude-files / --exclude-list entries are compared as raw strings; './'-prefixed, trailing-whitespace, '..'-containing, or symlink-differing entries silently exclude nothing
confirmedFindings.evidence: Producer side: exclude_files (Getopt::Yath PathList) stores the user string verbatim (no clean_path, no trim), and add_exclusions_from_lists (Finder.pm:116-118) splits list files on /\r?\n\r?/ and inserts each line into the EXCLUDE_FILES hash with no whitespace trim and no path normalization (verified by probe: entry 't/foo.t ' keeps its trailing space, './t/baz.t' keeps its ./ prefix). Consumer side: exclude_file (Finder.pm:726) does exact hash lookups against exactly two spellings: $full = clean_path($file, 0) (absolute, rel2abs, symlinks NOT resolved) and $rel = File::Spec->abs2rel($file) (App/Yath2/TestFile.pm:91, never './'-prefixed). Any other spelling — './t/x.t', 't/x.t ' (trailing space from an editor), 'x/../t/x.t', or an absolute path that differs by a symlinked component (realpath vs rel2abs) — matches neither key and the exclusion is a silent no-op. There is no 'exclusion entry matched nothing' report.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: User runs `yath test --exclude-list skip.txt t/` where skip.txt (edited on Windows or by a tool that pads lines) contains 't/destructive.t ' with a trailing space, or contains './t/destructive.t'. The lookup keys are 't/destructive.t' / '/abs/t/destructive.t', so nothing matches; t/destructive.t is scanned into the plan and RUNS anyway (against a production DB, in the destructive case). If it passes, exit code is 0 and the user never learns the exclusion was ignored.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Normalize both sides to one canonical form: trim leading/trailing whitespace (incl. \r) on every exclude entry, then store both clean_path($entry) and the abs2rel form as keys (skipping non-existent paths is fine — the entry is a name, not a file requirement). Optionally warn when an exclude entry never matched any discovered file.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Evidence correction: the split pattern /\r?\n\r?/ at Finder.pm:116 does handle CRLF, so "edited on Windows" (line endings) is NOT a trigger; drop that from the scenario. Real triggers verified: trailing/leading whitespace on a line, './'-prefixed entries (natural output of `find .` piped into an exclude list), '..'-containing paths, and absolute paths differing by a symlinked component (clean_path($file,0) skips realpath — Test2/Harness2/Util.pm:396-403). Same raw-string comparison also exists in the changes_exclude_files path (Finder.pm:248,256), not cited in the finding. Proposal stands: trim entries and canonicalize both sides (store both clean_path($entry) and abs2rel forms), optionally warn on exclude entries that matched nothing.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: No existing TODO_TASKS.md/TODO_STEPS.md ticket covers this specifically (grepped both files for "exclude" — only unrelated dist.ini/DB items found). Cheap mitigation matches the proposal almost exactly and is low-risk to land opportunistically: (1) trim leading/trailing whitespace (incl. \r) on each split line in add_exclusions_from_lists before inserting into EXCLUDE_FILES, and on the PathList constructor path; (2) in exclude_file, also normalize with clean_path on the entry side, or store an additional './'-stripped / trimmed key variant when building EXCLUDE_FILES so lookups are resilient to the common './' and whitespace variants. Symlink-vs-realpath is the hardest part to fully close (would need Cwd::realpath on both sides) and could be left as a known limitation. A one-line diagnostic ("N exclude entries never matched any discovered test file") would also cheaply surface the failure mode to users without needing full path-canonicalization.

confirmedFindings.title: Unvalidated HARNESS category/duration values (and durations-file values) pass client-side but hit an unguarded die in the runner's State, killing the whole runner process
confirmedFindings.evidence: Producer: App/Yath2/TestFile.pm:387-394 maps ANY non-long/medium/short directive token to $headers->{category} (e.g. '# HARNESS-CATEGORY-NETWORK' via Legacy.pm:231-239, or '# HARNESS2: category db'), and :381 stores ANY lowercased token as duration ('# HARNESS2: duration verylong'). Finder.pm:696 likewise feeds durations-JSON values into set_duration with no validation (a JSON of {"t/a.t": 12.4} — numeric seconds — yields duration '12.4'). queue_item emits these verbatim; RunPlan::populate and Client::submit_queue (Client.pm:505-509) forward them unchecked. Consumer: State::task_fields (State.pm:924-925) does `die "Invalid category: $cat" unless CATEGORIES->{$cat}` (only general/isolation/immiscible are valid, Constants.pm:11-12) and the same for duration. The die fires inside request_handler_queue_task -> submit_action -> state->queue_task (Handlers.pm:775-779, Runner.pm:883-895), and Role/Service.pm:382 dispatches handlers with NO eval — the exception unwinds the runner's service loop and the runner process dies. The E1 machinery (queue_item's directive_error synthetic-failure path, TestFile.pm:523-561) exists precisely to turn bad directives into one failed job, but only covers HARNESS2 grammar parse errors, not value-domain errors.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: One test in a 500-file suite carries `# HARNESS-CATEGORY-NETWORK` (a plausible-looking directive; the producer accepts it and queues it). During submit_queue the runner's queue_task handler dies 'Invalid category: network', the runner process exits, and the entire run aborts (or hangs the client until its liveness check trips) — every other test is taken down by one file's directive, with the diagnostic buried in the runner's death rather than attributed to the file. Same for `--durations db.json` whose values are numbers instead of SHORT/MEDIUM/LONG.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Validate category/duration against CATEGORIES/DURATIONS at the producer (App::Yath2::TestFile::check_category/check_duration or _apply_directives), routing invalid values through the existing directive_error E1 path so only that one job fails; additionally coerce/validate durations-file values in Finder (accept numeric seconds by thresholding into short/medium/long, or reject with a clear message naming the file).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: One imprecision: the runner process does not die uncaught. Runner.pm:474-477 wraps run_scheduler_only in eval, warns the exception, then performs orderly teardown (stop_preload_root/stop_sampler/teardown_plugins/stop/close_service) and returns exit code 1 (line 520). The client therefore sees the socket close as normal completion rather than hanging until a liveness check. Net effect is unchanged: one file's unrecognized-but-plausible directive value (or one numeric durations-JSON entry) aborts the entire run mid-submit, all other tests are killed or never started, and the diagnostic is a bare unattributed warn on the runner's stderr instead of a per-file failure.
confirmedFindings.severity_note: Severity is P1 rather than P0: this is a crash (not a hang/spin), triggered by user-authored test-file content that must deviate from the documented directive grammar (only long/medium/short are valid HARNESS-CATEGORY-* duration aliases; category free text must otherwise be general/isolation/immiscible) — plausible but not "common path" in the sense of arising from ordinary correct usage. Impact is nonetheless significant: because there's no eval anywhere between service_io (called from every iteration of the runner's main loops in Runner.pm) and the deep die site, one file's bad directive takes down the entire runner process, not just that job — and per MEMORY.md's project_service_architecture note, runners are persistent daemons, so this could abort other queued/in-flight runs sharing the same runner, not just the offending run. Cheap mitigation matches the finding's own proposal: validate category/duration at the producer (TestFile::check_category/check_duration or _apply_directives) and route failures through the existing E1 directive_error synthetic-failure path (TestFile.pm:523-561) so only the offending job fails; alternatively/additionally wrap the State.pm:922-925 dies (or the Service.pm request dispatch) in eval to at least turn a bad task into a failed-request response instead of a process-ending exception. No existing TODO_TASKS.md ticket found covering this specific gap.

confirmedFindings.title: --no-long / --only-long are evaluated before --durations data is applied, so durations-file LONG markings are silently ignored for selection
confirmedFindings.evidence: In find_project_files, exclusion runs at collection time: listed files at Finder.pm:637 and scanned files at :678 (include_file -> exclude_file), where :729-733 tests `$test->check_duration eq 'long'`. At that point check_duration sees only in-file headers (App/Yath2/TestFile.pm:166-179). The durations file/URL is fetched and applied to the surviving @tests only afterwards, at Finder.pm:686-698 ($test->set_duration(...)). The --durations option is documented as 'This will override durations listed in the file headers' (Options/Finder.pm:673), but for the no_long/only_long selection decision it never can: a test marked LONG only in the durations source is judged 'medium' when the exclude decision is made.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: durations.json marks t/huge.t as LONG (t/huge.t itself has no in-file directive). `yath test --durations durations.json --no-long t/` still runs t/huge.t (exit 0) — the flag the user relied on to skip slow tests silently doesn't apply. Worse inversion: `yath test --durations durations.json --only-long t/` EXCLUDES t/huge.t (it reads 'medium' at exclusion time) and selects only tests with an in-file LONG directive — potentially zero tests, with no hint that the durations data was ignored for selection.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Fetch/apply duration data (or at least consult it) before the exclude_file pass: e.g. resolve duration_data first, pass it into exclude_file, or split collection from filtering so set_duration happens between them.
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Two additions: (1) The identical ordering exists in legacy 1.x (reference/legacy/lib/Test2/Harness/Finder.pm — exclude at :634/:675, set_duration at :693), so this is a long-standing inherited bug rather than a 2.0d regression; fix should probably be considered for the evolve line deliberately. (2) A further gate the finding missed: the durations source is only fetched when durations_threshold passes (Finder.pm:687-688, `if ($threshold && $test_count >= $threshold)`); threshold defaults to job_count+1 (Options/Finder.pm:771-778), so on runs with fewer tests than jobs+1 an explicit --durations file is silently ignored even for scheduling — widening the finding. Proposal stands: resolve duration_data and apply set_duration (or consult the durations hash) before/inside the exclude_file pass, e.g. split collection from filtering.

confirmedFindings.title: Listed-vs-scanned dedup uses rel2abs without realpath, so a symlink-aliased or '..'-containing explicit path queues the same test file twice
confirmedFindings.evidence: Explicitly listed files are keyed into %seen as clean_path($path, 0) (Finder.pm:629-630) and scanned files as clean_path($File::Find::name, 0) (:663-665); clean_path with $absolute=0 skips realpath and only does File::Spec->rel2abs (Test2/Harness2/Util.pm:396-403). rel2abs/canonpath does NOT collapse '..' and does not resolve symlinks (verified: rel2abs('t/../t/foo.t') stays '/cwd/t/../t/foo.t'). So the same physical file listed under an aliased spelling and also discovered by the directory scan produces two different %seen keys, two TestFile objects, and two tasks in RunPlan::populate — the file runs twice in one run.
confirmedFindings.failure_scenario: `yath test t/../t/db.t t/` (shell-completion or Makefile-generated path) or `yath test link/db.t t/` where `link -> t`: db.t is queued twice with different job_ids, runs twice concurrently — for a test that grabs an exclusive resource (port, db schema) protected only by its HARNESS-CONFLICTS marker being deduped per-file, the second copy races the first and both can fail flakily; even when both pass, the summary double-counts the file and exit stays 0 with no dedup warning.
confirmedFindings.proposal: Key %seen on clean_path($path) with realpath enabled (the default $absolute=1) for both the listed and File::Find branches (keep the non-realpath form as the task's file path if desired — only the dedup key needs canonicalization).
confirmedFindings.accuracy_note: Scope the fix to the dedup key only: compute a realpath-canonical key (clean_path($path) default) for %seen in both branches while keeping the existing non-realpath path as the TestFile's file (as the proposal's parenthetical suggests). Fully realpath-ing the stored path would change what plugins' claim_file sees and would collapse projects that intentionally symlink one test under multiple names within the scan tree. Also note the fully-realpath dedup key means a listed symlink alias will suppress the scanned canonical copy (or vice versa) — acceptable, but worth a dedup notice when a listed path is skipped.
